summary: Both of Tony's bug reports trace to concrete, evidenced gaps in main-process lifecycle wiring, not bad luck. (1) The single-instance-lock model (index.ts:8785-8797) has no liveness check, so a wedged-but-not-exited first instance holds the OS lock forever and a relaunch silently self-quits with zero user feedback; separately the renderer's 'unresponsive' handler (index.ts:2722-2726) only logs and never recovers, leaving only an undiscoverable, macOS-only, main-thread-dependent emergency shortcut as the escape hatch. Together these are the exact mechanism behind "History sometimes just doesn't open the app again; it's running but frozen." (2) Sidecar cleanup (llama-server, fm-serve, and a newly-identified gap: the ffmpeg import-decoder child process) is 100% JS-event-driven via will-quit/forceQuitMétis and has zero OS-level safety net and zero boot-time reaping of stray processes from a previous run -- so any external Force Quit, native crash, or OS-level kill (which E3's 8-same-day-relaunches-with-no-clean-shutdown evidence shows is the dominant real exit pattern for this install) leaves the 3.3GB local-LLM sidecar running forever, exactly matching the observed orphaned llama-server processes and directly substantiating "very heavy on the PC." Beyond the two P0 root causes, index.ts is a 9,518-line God Module and its registerIpc() function is a single 4,147-line closure holding ~160 IPC handlers across a dozen unrelated domains -- the concrete #1 refactor target, for which the report includes a full line-ranged decomposition map into ~30 cohesive modules. Positive findings: BrowserWindow webPreferences are correctly hardened (sandbox/contextIsolation/no-nodeIntegration), IPC sender validation is essentially complete (161/163 handlers verified gated, the other 2 hand-confirmed as false positives in the sweep), boot-sentinel.ts is a clean, well-reasoned module, and the historical background-screen-capture retry loop (E5) appears already fixed at HEAD via MQA-209 gating.

findings.title: Single-instance lock has no liveness check -- a wedged (not exited) instance permanently swallows relaunches with zero user feedback
findings.evidence: index.ts:8785-8797: `if (!app.requestSingleInstanceLock()) { app.quit() } else { app.on('second-instance', () => { const w = ensureWindow(); if (!w) return; if (!w.isVisible()) w.showInactive() }) }`. Electron's lock is a pure OS-process-existence check; 'second-instance' delivery requires the lock-holding process's own JS event loop to dequeue and run the callback. A second launch that fails to acquire the lock takes the bare app.quit() branch with no dialog, notification, or any user-visible signal.
findings.failure_scenario: Main process stalls on any synchronous long-running IPC handler body (there are ~160 of them) while the lock is held; a relaunch (dock icon, Start Menu, second click) silently no-ops because it can't acquire the lock and the frozen holder never processes 'second-instance' either. User sees: nothing happens, existing window still frozen -- exactly 'when I click on History sometimes it just doesn't open the app again; it's running but it just freezes.'
findings.fix_direction: Add a liveness heartbeat the lock-holder writes periodically (or answer a bounded-timeout ping over IPC); a relaunch that gets no response within ~2-3s should tell the user plainly, kill the stale PID, and proceed to boot normally (letting boot-sentinel's own recovery do its job). Needs a planning pass for the timeout/UX, not a one-line patch.

verification.evidence:
The code is where the finding says: src/main/index.ts:8785-8797 is `if (!app.requestSingleInstanceLock()) { app.quit() } else { app.on('second-instance', () => { const w = ensureWindow(); if (!w) return; if (!w.isVisible()) w.showInactive() }) }`, and the losing branch gives the user no feedback. The mechanism behind the finding is wrong, though, and it is wrong on Tony's own platform (macOS).

1) The claim that the lock is "a pure OS-process-existence check" is false. I read the Chromium source that Electron 43.6.0 is built on (electron DEPS: chromium_version 150.0.7871.250), file chrome/browser/process_singleton_posix.cc, which is also used on macOS:
- A second process connects to the SingletonSocket, sends START, then waits up to kTimeoutInSeconds=20 for an ACK (line 137, `ReadFromSocketWithTimeout(..., timeout)`).
- The ACK is sent from LinuxWatcher::HandleMessage, which runs on the UI thread (it checks `ui_task_runner_->BelongsToCurrentThread()`). That is the thread running the JS event loop and Electron's second-instance callback (electron_api_app.cc NotificationCallbackWrapper, line 433).
- If no ACK arrives (lines 913-918): `if (!kill_unresponsive || !KillProcessByLockPath(true)) return PROFILE_IN_USE; ... return PROCESS_NONE`. NotifyOtherProcessWithTimeoutOrCreate always passes kill_unresponsive=true. KillProcessByLockPath then calls KillProcess, which sends SIGKILL to the pid in SingletonLock. The new process then calls Create() and takes the lock.

Neither of Electron's ProcessSingleton patches (process_singleton.patch, feat_add_data_parameter_to_processsingleton.patch, both at v43.6.0) changes this posix no-ACK kill path. So on macOS a wedged holder does not "permanently swallow" relaunches. A real second process waits about 20 s and then SIGKILLs it.

2) On macOS the lock is usually not involved at all. electron-builder.yml:227 sets `LSUIElement: true`. Relaunching an app that is already running (Finder, Spotlight, Launchpad) does not start a second process: LaunchServices sends a reopen Apple Event to the running process, which Electron delivers as `app.on('activate')` (index.ts:9410). That handler runs on the same main thread. If that thread is blocked, the click does nothing, however the lock is designed. Tony's "running but frozen, won't reopen" symptom on his Mac is a hung main thread (or renderer), not a lock defect.

3) On Windows the finding mostly holds. chrome_process_finder.cc:33,90 uses SendMessageTimeout with a 20 s timeout. When that returns kWindowHung and any visible window exists (process_singleton_win.cc:311-325), it calls should_kill_remote_process_callback_. Electron's patch replaces DisplayShouldKillMessageBox with `return false`, so the result is PROCESS_NOTIFIED ("Quit silently"). requestSingleInstanceLock then returns false and index.ts:8786 runs app.quit(). So on Windows, a hung Métis with a visible overlay silently swallows every relaunch after a 20 s wait, for as long as it stays hung.

4) The claim of "~160 synchronous long-running IPC handler bodies" is unsupported. index.ts has 164 `ipcMain.handle/on` registrations, but nothing shows they are synchronous or long-running.

5) Side note on the lead's evidence E3: there is no clean-shutdown audit event anywhere. The app.* audit types in src/main/logger.ts are only started, renderer.ready, act1.dom, crash, recovery, boot.watch_cleared and unresponsive. So "no clean-shutdown events between app.started" does not by itself prove force-quits.

6) Related observation that fits E2: when the macOS singleton path SIGKILLs a hung holder, will-quit never runs (index.ts:9461-9517 localRuntime.stop()/fmRuntime.stop()). That kill, like any force-quit, leaves llama-server orphaned under ppid=1. That is a separate finding (sidecars do not reap themselves), not this one.
verification.corrected_mechanism_or_fix:
Corrected mechanism: the single-instance lock does have a liveness check built into Chromium: a 20 s wait for an ACK that the main/UI thread must send.
- macOS/posix: a second process that gets no ACK SIGKILLs the hung holder and boots normally. In practice Tony's relaunches never create a second process anyway: LSUIElement plus LaunchServices sends a reopen/activate event to the existing, hung process. So the lock is not the root cause of "History freezes, app won't reopen". The root cause is whatever blocks the Electron main thread (or the overlay renderer) after History is clicked, and that needs its own trace.
- Windows: Electron's patched DisplayShouldKillMessageBox returns false. A hung holder with any visible window gets a silent PROCESS_NOTIFIED, and the second launch quits without feedback after about 20 s. The finding's UX complaint is valid there only.

Fix direction, replacing the proposed custom heartbeat:
(a) Do not build a parallel heartbeat or lock. Chromium already does this check.
(b) Treat the main-thread stall as the P0/P1 root cause. Instrument it with a worker_threads watchdog that pings the main loop and writes an audit event (e.g. app.main_stall with duration and the last IPC channel) when it gets no reply for more than N seconds. Then find and fix the History IPC path that blocks.
(c) Windows UX: in the lock-fail branch at index.ts:8785, time the requestSingleInstanceLock() call. If it took about 19 s or more, the holder was hung. Show a dialog offering to force-quit the stale instance (pid from the lock/tasklist) and relaunch, instead of a silent app.quit().
(d) Separately, make the llama-server and fm-serve sidecars reap themselves when the parent dies (parent-pid/stdin-EOF watchdog, or a boot-time sweep of pidfiles). Both the singleton SIGKILL and force-quit skip will-quit, which is what leaves them orphaned (E2).

findings.title: 'unresponsive' renderer event only logs -- no recovery, no UI-surfaced escape hatch, and the one escape hatch (Cmd+Opt+Esc) is macOS-only and depends on main thread being alive
findings.evidence: index.ts:2719-2730: win.on('unresponsive', () => { ...mainLog.warn(...); auditLog('app.unresponsive', {kind:'overlay'}) }) -- no reload, no destroy+recreate, no dialog. index.ts:4214-4224 registerEmergencyForceQuitShortcut returns false unconditionally when process.platform !== 'darwin' -- no Windows equivalent exists at all. The shortcut itself is a globalShortcut callback that still needs the main process event loop to run it.
findings.failure_scenario: E6: render-process-gone reason=killed exitCode=15 followed 5s later by app.unresponsive kind=overlay -- the crash-recovery reload (index.ts:2737-2783) itself produces a renderer that then hangs, with no further escalation beyond another log line. On Windows there is no equivalent recovery affordance at all.
findings.fix_direction: After N consecutive unresponsive events or one exceeding a grace period, destroy+recreate the BrowserWindow (reuse the existing crash-recovery logic at 2737-2783). Surface the escape hatch in the tray menu once app.unresponsive fires, and add a cross-platform (not darwin-only) recovery affordance.

verification.evidence:
Read at origin/main 2bf21f1c, src/main/index.ts (9518 lines).

What holds up:
- index.ts:2722-2726 matches the finding. `win.on('unresponsive')` only calls mainLog.warn and auditLog('app.unresponsive', {kind:'overlay'}). It does not reload, recreate the window or show a dialog.
- index.ts:2727-2730: 'responsive' goes to mainLog only, with no audit event. So audit.log cannot show whether the E6 stall ever recovered.
- index.ts:4214-4215: registerEmergencyForceQuitShortcut returns false when the platform is not darwin.
- index.ts:8788-8797: the second-instance handler only calls ensureWindow() and showInactive(). A relaunch while the renderer is wedged just shows the frozen window again, which fits Tony's "running but frozen" report.

What is wrong:
1. No auto-recovery is a deliberate choice, and a test enforces it. The comment at index.ts:2719-2721 says Chromium recovers most stalls and a forced reload mid-meeting would drop the live transcript. src/main/bank-grade-hardening.contract.test.ts:37-45 asserts the handler must NOT match loadURL, loadFile, reload, destroy, app.exit, app.quit or relaunch. The suggested fix ("destroy+recreate after N events") would fail that test and throw away the transcript this design protects.
2. "No Windows equivalent exists at all" is false. The tray menu (index.ts:4418-4422) has a 'Force Quit Métis' item on every platform with click: forceQuitMétis. Only the accelerator label is darwin-only. forceQuitMétis (index.ts:4195-4212) tries a graceful quit, hard-exits after 4 s, and stops sidecars via stopSidecarsForHardExit (4170-4193). Suggesting "surface the escape hatch in the tray" is therefore wrong: it is already there on all platforms.
3. The shortcut is misnamed. The app's accelerator is Command+Control+Escape (index.ts:4154). Cmd+Opt+Esc is macOS's own Force Quit, which the comment at 4150-4153 names as the fallback when main itself hangs.
4. "Depends on the main thread being alive" mixes up two failures. The 'unresponsive' event is about a renderer hang, and during a renderer hang the main process is alive, so the tray item and the shortcut both work. A main-process hang is a separate failure that no in-app handler can fix.
5. The E6 mechanism is not proven. It claims "the crash-recovery reload produces a renderer that then hangs". A freshly reloaded renderer is unlikely to trip Chromium's hang monitor (much longer than 5 s, from memory) within 5 s. Separately, Electron's BrowserWindow close path schedules its own 5000 ms unresponsive event when a close or quit doesn't finish (from memory of Electron's source; not checked here). The exact 5 s gap after a SIGTERM kill (exitCode 15) fits a shutdown or close sequence at least as well as a hang after recovery. This is inference, not observed. The link to the History freeze is also unproven: no code path ties History to this handler.

Real gap left over: there is no user-triggered, non-destructive way to recover a wedged renderer. The tray only offers Force Quit or Quit, and other tray items (Settings, New) send IPC into the dead renderer. A relaunch does not recover it either. With a cross-platform escape already in place, a deliberate test-pinned trade-off and an unproven causal link, this is P2, not P0. It rises to P1 if the History freeze turns out to be a renderer wedge.
verification.corrected_mechanism_or_fix:
Keep the "no automatic reload" rule, since it is test-pinned and protects a live transcript. Add recovery that the user explicitly triggers instead:
(a) Keep a module flag `overlayUnresponsive`. Set it in the 'unresponsive' handler at index.ts:2722 and clear it in 'responsive'. Also emit auditLog('app.responsive') so audit.log shows whether stalls recover.
(b) In the second-instance handler (index.ts:8788), if overlayUnresponsive is true, treat the relaunch as the user's recovery gesture. Either reload with the same state-reset block the render-process-gone path uses at 2737-2783 (factor that block into a shared recoverOverlayRenderer(self)), or show a native dialog.showMessageBox (main process, cross-platform) with "Wait / Reload window / Quit".
(c) Add a tray item "Reload window" in buildTrayMenu (index.ts:4393+) that calls the same helper, available on all platforms.
Tests: update bank-grade-hardening.contract.test.ts so it still asserts the 'unresponsive' handler never reloads by itself, and add tests that second-instance and the tray item do reload when the flag is set.
Separately, find the History freeze's own root cause (which main IPC or renderer work History triggers), because this handler only records the symptom. Check E6 against Electron's 5 s close-timeout behaviour before calling it a hang after recovery.

findings.title: Sidecar-process cleanup is 100% JS-event-driven with no OS-level safety net and no boot-time reaping; ffmpeg import-decoder child process is missing from even the JS-level kill list
findings.evidence: will-quit (index.ts:9461-9518) and stopSidecarsForHardExit (index.ts:4164-4212) each call screenPreprocess.stop()/localRuntime.stop()/fmRuntime.stop() but are never reached on an external SIGKILL, a native crash bypassing V8 (the exact MQA-175 class boot-sentinel.ts documents), or an OS watchdog kill. Separately, ffmpeg-decoder.ts spawns real ffmpeg children (spawn at lines 37/110) whose only kill path (closeImportDecoder, index.ts:1317-1354, cancel() at ffmpeg-decoder.ts:57/192) is invoked from job-completion/IPC paths but never from will-quit or stopSidecarsForHardExit -- grep for ffmpegDecoders/decoderWin in both quit-path bodies returns nothing. No boot-time scan reaps a stray llama-server/fm-serve process left by a previous run either.
findings.failure_scenario: E3 shows 8 app.started events in one day with zero clean-shutdown events between them (repeated Force Quit/crash/relaunch). Each such exit leaves the 3.3GB qwen GGUF llama-server (and/or fm-serve, and/or an in-flight ffmpeg decode) running indefinitely -- exactly E2's two orphaned llama-server processes (ppid=1, alive longer than the current main process), and the direct explanation for 'it's very heavy on the PC' as dead-process sidecars accumulate across restarts.
findings.fix_direction: Two layers: (1) OS-level containment -- process-group/Job-Object (Windows JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE) or a tiny watchdog that self-kills when its parent PID changes, so cleanup doesn't depend on any JS event firing; (2) boot-time reaping of any stray sidecar from a previous run, recorded alongside the existing MQA-175 boot-sentinel file, ship first as the smaller/lower-risk change. Also add the ffmpeg decoder to both existing quit-path kill lists immediately.

verification.evidence:
I read the code at HEAD 2bf21f1c. The core claim holds, but three parts of the finding need correcting.

What I confirmed:
- `src/main/llm/local-runtime.ts:362-366` spawns llama-server with `spawn(binaryPath, args, {stdio:['ignore','pipe','pipe'], windowsHide:true, env})`. It passes no `detached` option, no process group, no Job Object and no parent-PID argument.
- `buildSpawnArgs` (lines 172-199) uses `--port 0`, and the API key is random per session (line 226). So a llama-server left behind by an earlier run can't be reached or reused by a new instance. It is pure waste.
- The only kill is `stopChildProcess()` / `stop()` at lines 625-639 (SIGKILL). The 15-minute idle stop (lines 64 and 296) is a timer in the parent, so it dies with the parent. An idle orphan writes nothing to its stdout/stderr pipe, so it never gets EPIPE/SIGPIPE and lives forever. That matches E2 (ppid=1, alive for about 14 hours).
- `fm-runtime.ts:285-286` has the same pattern, with its kill at lines 369-373.
- `localRuntime.stop()` and `fmRuntime.stop()` are called only from `will-quit` (`index.ts:9461-9518`) and `stopSidecarsForHardExit` (`index.ts:4164-4212`). The latter runs only on the Cmd+Ctrl+Esc emergency-quit path.
- No boot-time reaper exists. Grep for pgrep/pkill/killall/pidfile/`ps` in `src/main` finds only Windows `taskkill` for CLI trees in `cli.ts`. `boot-sentinel.ts` tracks only the Electron PID and minidumps, not sidecar PIDs.
- So macOS Force Quit (SIGKILL), a native crash (E7 minidumps), or a watchdog kill leaves llama-server and fm-serve orphaned. Reachable in production.

What the finding missed (a gap you can fix in JS today):
- `onFatal` at `index.ts:3574-3576` does `app.relaunch(); app.exit(0)` when the user picks "Relaunch Métis" in the crash dialog.
- `app.exit()` never emits `will-quit`, and this path does not call `stopSidecarsForHardExit()`.
- So every crash-dialog relaunch leaves a running llama-server behind, deterministically.

Corrections:
1. **The E3 inference doesn't hold.** No clean-shutdown audit event exists at all. `logger.ts:203-217` lists only `app.started`, `app.renderer.ready`, `app.act1.dom`, `app.crash`, `app.recovery`, `app.boot.watch_cleared` and `app.unresponsive`, and `will-quit` writes none of them. So "8 app.started with no clean-shutdown events" doesn't prove force-quits. E2 (the orphaned processes seen directly) is the real evidence.
2. **The ffmpeg part is overstated.** It's true that `ffmpegDecoders` and `decoderWin` are absent from both quit bodies. But `ffmpeg-decoder.ts:110-113` has ffmpeg writing continuously to `pipe:1`. When the parent dies, the pipe closes and ffmpeg exits on EPIPE. The duration probe (line 37) is bounded by `-t 0`. So ffmpeg doesn't pile up as a long-lived orphan. This is a P3 cleanup item, not part of the "heavy on PC" cause.
3. **Severity P0 -> P1.** It needs an abnormal exit to trigger, and it doesn't cause the History freeze or crash itself. It does add one multi-GB process (model weights plus KV cache for a 65536 context) per abnormal exit, and it is the best-supported explanation for Tony's "very heavy on the PC" report.
4. **Line 626 is roughly right.** `stopChildProcess` is at line 625 and `stop()` at line 632.
verification.corrected_mechanism_or_fix:
Mechanism: sidecars are ordinary piped children, and the app only kills them from two JS quit paths.
- Any exit that skips both paths leaves llama-server and fm-serve running forever, holding RAM: SIGKILL/Force Quit, a native crash, or the `onFatal` relaunch (`app.exit(0)` at `index.ts:3576`).
- The idle-stop timer dies with the parent.
- The new instance can't find or reuse the orphan, because it listens on a random port and needs a per-session key.

Fix, in this order:
1. **One-line fix now.** Call `stopSidecarsForHardExit()` before `app.relaunch(); app.exit(0)` in `onFatal` (`index.ts:3574-3576`). Add a contract test that every `app.exit` call site is preceded by the sidecar teardown.
2. **Boot-time reaping.** On each spawn, write `userData/sidecars.json` with pid, the absolute binary path and the start time, and delete it on `stop()`. Early in boot, next to `boot-sentinel`, read that file. For each pid that is still alive and whose executable (`ps -p <pid> -o comm=` on macOS, the image path on Windows) matches the bundled llama-server or fm-serve path, send SIGKILL. The path match guards against PID reuse. This is the smallest change and would have cleaned up both E2 orphans.
3. **OS-level containment.**
   - Windows: put children in a Job Object with `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE`.
   - macOS: launch through a tiny supervisor that polls the original parent pid (`kill -0`) and SIGKILLs the child when the parent is gone, for example `sh -c` with the child in the background plus a 2-second `kill -0` loop. The llama-server binary is pinned and can't be changed to watch stdin EOF.
4. **ffmpeg hygiene (P3).** In `will-quit` and `stopSidecarsForHardExit`, loop over `ffmpegDecoders` and call `.cancel()` on each. This is for tidiness only; ffmpeg already exits on EPIPE when the parent's pipe closes.

findings.title: readEvalMetrics() does a synchronous full-file read+parse of the audit log on the main thread
findings.evidence: metrics.ts:107-126: readFileSync(path, 'utf8').trim().split('\n') reads the ENTIRE audit.log (up to the 5MB rotation cap set in logger.ts:35) before slicing to the last 10,000 lines, then JSON.parse's each. Runs synchronously on the single main-process JS thread whenever the metrics IPC handler fires.
findings.failure_scenario: On a slow/network/AV-scanned disk, or with a realistic 5MB audit.log (E4/E5/E8 all show high audit volume), this blocks every pending IPC handler and timer for the read+parse duration -- a measurable main-thread stall the instant a metrics view is opened, compounding the overlay's perceived 'freeze'.
findings.fix_direction: Move to a worker_thread, or replace the full-file read with a bounded reverse-seek/tail read since only the last N lines are ever used.

verification.evidence:
The code is where the finding says, but the impact claim does not hold up.

1. The mechanism is real. In /Users/<redacted-user>/AI-Brain-build/metis-2.0/src/main/metrics.ts:107-126 (HEAD 2bf21f1c), readEvalMetrics() calls `readFileSync(path, 'utf8').trim().split('\n')` at line 111, which reads the whole audit.log. It then does `lines.slice(-maxLines)` with maxLines = 10_000 and JSON.parse's each line, all synchronously. Its only caller is the ipcMain.handle(IPC.metricsRead) handler at src/main/index.ts:8412-8416, which runs on the main process, so the work does run on the main JS thread.

2. The rotation-cap citation is wrong. logger.ts:35 sets the 5MB cap on the MAIN diagnostic log. The audit log's 5MB cap is at logger.ts:63 (`audit.transports.file.maxSize = 5 * 1024 * 1024`). The practical upper bound is still about 5MB.

3. It only runs when a user opens a specific screen. The one renderer caller is DiagnosticsSection in src/renderer/src/components/Settings.tsx:7558-7580. It calls window.toto.readMetrics() once when it mounts and again when the Retry button is clicked. It is only rendered in the Settings 'about' tab (Settings.tsx:7373-7381). Nothing polls it or calls it on a timer, it is not called at startup, and it is not on the History path. The handler is also skipped when the user is not signed in (requireAuth).

4. The measured cost is small. On Tony's Mac, userData/logs holds audit.log (2.1MB, 11,950 lines) and audit.old.log (5.0MB, 22,637 lines). I ran the exact read, trim, split, slice(-10000) and JSON.parse loop on the 5MB file in node, five times: 9.4 to 11.7 ms per run. That is one pause of about 10 ms, once per visit to Settings > About. It is well below anything a user would notice as a freeze.

5. It has no link to the reported bugs. The freeze and crash reports (E2, E3, E6, E9) and the heavy-CPU report (E4, E5) come from other code paths. This handler cannot cause the "click History, app freezes" symptom, and it adds nothing to steady-state load.
verification.corrected_mechanism_or_fix:
Corrected mechanism: when the user opens Settings > About, DiagnosticsSection mounts and calls metrics:read once. The handler does a synchronous read of the whole live audit.log (capped at 5MB by logger.ts:63, not :35), splits it, and JSON.parse's the last 10k lines on the main thread. Measured on the real 5MB file this takes about 10 ms, once per open. It is a small inefficiency that happens only when the user asks for it. It is not a freeze contributor, so it should be P3, not P1.

Optional cheap fix (a worker_thread is overkill): open the file with fs.promises.open, stat it, and read only the last ~2-3MB (10k lines at ~180 B/line is about 1.8MB) from an offset. Drop the first partial line, then parse. Or make the handler async with fs.promises.readFile so the disk I/O leaves the main thread. Either one bounds the cost regardless of file size.

Side note, not part of this finding: metrics only reads the live audit.log, not the rotated generations. The numbers therefore drop after each rotation, which is a correctness gap. Also, Tony's userData has audit.old.log rather than audit-<epoch>.log. That suggests the custom archiveLogFn in logger.ts:71 may not be what rotated this file, and it may be worth checking in a separate lane.

findings.title: registerIpc() is a single 4,147-line function registering ~160 IPC handlers across a dozen unrelated domains
findings.evidence: index.ts:4624-8771, confirmed as one function body (no other top-level function boundary in that range). Handlers grouped by IPC-name prefix: brain*(18), import*(13), recall*(12), window*(10), mcp*(8), dust*(7), cloud*(6), cli*(6), member*(5), license*(4), graphify*(4), plus ~30 more prefixes, all sharing one closure scope and the module-level mutable state (win, tray, decoderWin, ffmpegDecoders, importJobs, speakerIdInstance, ...).

verification.evidence:
I parsed src/main/index.ts at 2bf21f1 with the repo's own TypeScript compiler API. Every factual claim in the finding holds. Only the severity is too high.

**Size and handler count.**
- `function registerIpc(): void` runs from line 4624 to line 8771. That is 4,148 lines out of 9,518 in the file.
- The next-largest top-level function is createWindow at 346 lines.
- The body has 159 `ipcMain.handle` and 4 `ipcMain.on` calls. Only one other ipcMain call exists in the file (a dynamic `ipcMain.handle(channel, ...)` near line 9161).
- The prefix counts match the finding exactly: brain 18, import 13, recall 12, window 10, mcp 8, dust 7, cli 6, cloud 6, member 5, license 4, graphify 4, plus about 30 smaller prefixes.
- No other non-test file under src/main registers IPC, so no per-domain split exists yet.

**Shared module-level state.** Confirmed at these lines:
- `speakerIdInstance` :253
- `win` / `tray` :984-985
- `importJobs` :1108

findings.title: Boot-time local-model prewarm eligibility ignores background-ingest routing, leaving E4's cold-start burst unwarmed

findings.failure_scenario: On a profile where local is effective primary for background ingest but useFor.suggest is off and a cloud provider is otherwise configured, the boot-time prewarm (both the immediate and 4s-backstop paths) skips warming, and the ~20-job ingest burst that fires within 200ms of launch (E4) pays the full 30-41s llama-server cold start on its first extraction job -- matching E4's observed sequence exactly (brain.consolidation+ingest burst, then local.runtime.start, then llm.call ttaMs 41282/29637).

verification.evidence:
The code gap the reviewer names is real, but the failure scenario does not hold, it does not explain E4, and P1 is too high.

What checks out in the code:
- src/main/llm/local-routing.ts:185-214 `localPrewarmEligible` returns true on exactly three conditions: `useFor.suggest`; `resilience.hedge && localLlm.fallback`; or `fallback && !cloudReady`. It never checks the ingest routing.
- src/main/brain/ingest.ts:106-186 `pickProviderCandidates` makes local the only candidate when `intelligenceRequiresLocal(s)` is true (src/shared/intelligence-pass.ts:16-17: `useFor.summary || routingMode==='local' || brainConsolidation.preferLocal`). Otherwise local is added last, as a fallback.
- ingest.ts:1405-1406 `extractConcurrency` and index.ts:8864-8884 `warmLocalIfReady` read as the reviewer says. The provisioning path and the 4 s backstop (`setTimeout(warmLocalIfReady, 4000)`) are both gated only on `localPrewarmEligible`.

Why the gap is narrow:
- `resilience.hedge` defaults to true (src/shared/ipc.ts:1325 and 1637).
- The `fallback` schema comment (ipc.ts:1289) says Settings turns `fallback` on when the user enables Local.
- So on a typical profile with Local on, branch 2 (`hedge && fallback`) already makes prewarm eligible. The gap only opens when the user has turned hedge or fallback off while cloud is ready.

Where the failure scenario breaks down:
1. Boot brain work does not start within 200 ms of launch. It starts in index.ts:9347's `setTimeout(..., 15_000)`, which runs `resumeBackfillIfPending` / `reconcileMeetingsInBackground` / catch-up. That is 11 s after the 4 s prewarm backstop.
2. The ~20-event "burst" is `brain.ingest` completion events, which `finishJob` logs after extraction (ingest.ts:1725). They are about 8 ms apart with no `llm.call` between them. These are reconcile jobs that reuse a saved extraction (ingest.ts:1697-1702), so they make no LLM call and pay no cold start.
3. audit.log does not match the scenario:
   - 17:47:07 launch: consolidation ran at 17:54:11, seven minutes later. The single `llm.call` that paid the cold start (ttaMs 41282) was running at that moment.
   - 18:03:25 launch: the extraction call started at about 18:03:40 (+15.2 s).
   - 18:10:20 launch: the extraction call started at about 18:10:35 (+15.1 s) but waited only 16.9 s. `local.runtime.start` (logged once the runtime is healthy, local-runtime.ts:557) came at 18:10:52. So the runtime was already starting before the 15 s step. Something already warms it at boot on Tony's profile, most likely the boot prewarm.
4. The extraction job starts the runtime itself anyway (local.ts:194 `ensureLocalRuntimeStarted` in `streamLocal`). The added branch would give at most about 11 s of head start on a 30-41 s load, for background work nobody is waiting on. It would also spend more speculative RAM, which cuts against Tony's "very heavy" report.
5. I found no path from this gap to the History freeze. The work is async, and it happens in the child process and the background ingest queue.

What the cold start is actually made of (from the code and files on disk):
- On every stopped-to-start transition, local.ts:66-68 runs `verifyIntegrity` (local-models.ts:478-492). That re-hashes both model files with SHA-256 via `hashFile` (local-models.ts:452-461).
- The files are the qwen3.5-4b model.gguf (2,912,109,728 B) and mmproj.gguf (672,423,616 B), about 3.58 GB in total. Every chunk goes through `hash.update` on the main-process event loop.
- llama-server then loads a 2.9 GB 4B model.
- `IDLE_STOP_MS` is 15 min (local-runtime.ts:64), so this repeats after every idle gap. That fits E8 (62 starts).

Unverified: `PREWARM_MIN_FREE_RAM_GB` is 4 and is checked against `os.freemem()`. On macOS that value is often under 4 GB, which could skip unattended warms for a different reason. I could not read Tony's settings or live free RAM because settings.json is encrypted.
verification.corrected_mechanism_or_fix:
Corrected mechanism:
- `localPrewarmEligible` does ignore the ingest route (`intelligenceRequiresLocal`: `useFor.summary`, `routingMode 'local'`, `brainConsolidation.preferLocal`). That only matters when hedge or fallback is off.
- It is not what drives E4. Boot extraction starts 15 s after launch (index.ts:9347), and the ~20 fast `brain.ingest` events make no LLM call.
- The 17-41 s waits come from the cold start itself:
  - a full SHA-256 re-hash of the 3.58 GB qwen3.5-4b model + mmproj on the main-process event loop (local.ts:66-68 → local-models.ts:452-492);
  - then loading the 2.9 GB model;
  - repeated after every 15-minute idle stop (local-runtime.ts:64).

Recommended fix:
- Do not add a fourth prewarm branch. It adds standing RAM and makes the "heavy on the PC" complaint worse.
- Cache the integrity result, keyed by path + size + mtime + inode (or a persisted verified marker written after download). Re-hash only when the file changes.
- If a re-hash is still needed, move it off the main thread (worker_threads) or at least batch it.
- Consider a longer idle stop, or skip the idle stop while background ingest work is still queued.
- Consider whether the 4B model should be the default on this hardware.
- Check whether `os.freemem()` on macOS keeps `PREWARM_MIN_FREE_RAM_GB` (4) from ever passing.
- If a warm for ingest is still wanted, make it part of the 15 s boot brain step: call `ensureLocalRuntimeStarted` only when `pickProviderCandidates(s)[0]?.provider === 'local'` and there are jobs that need an LLM. Do not widen `localPrewarmEligible` for it.

summary: This lane (meetings/transcripts/brain history data model, ~22.2k LOC) is unusually well-engineered for a codebase under real production stress — atomic writes, per-file mtime+size caches, two correctly-separated write-serialization lanes, and dozens of inline comments citing specific prior audit fixes (MQA-xxx/MI-x). The centerpiece finding connects code to Tony's real, live disk: .brain/index.json on his actual meetings folder (~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-MantuGroup/Métis Meetings, 360 files/892K, confirmed via resolveMeetingsFolder in transcripts.ts) has been quarantined as corrupt/undecryptable 178 times between 2026-08-20 and 2026-09-23, accelerating sharply (64 events on 09-23 alone), plus 18 orphaned .tmp files never swept. Code tracing shows this is not cosmetic: brain/store.ts's quarantineUnusableIndex resets the ingest ledger to empty on every such event, and brain/ingest.ts's startBackfill/reconcileMeetingsInBackground (armed at boot and every 60s) then treat every real meeting as unprocessed and requeue the whole vault for re-merge/re-extraction — a mechanism that plausibly explains both 'heavy on my PC' (repeated reconcile storms + cold local-LLM starts, matching the lead's E4 runtime evidence almost exactly) and contributes to the instability behind 'History doesn't open.' The write path itself (writeSaved, tmp+rename) is verified atomic, so the root trigger of the corruption remains an open question (two candidate mechanisms identified: transient keychain/safeStorage unavailability post-crash, or OneDrive Files-On-Demand interaction) — that needs one more log-correlation pass, which was outside this lane's authorized evidence (audit.log/mainLog). A second, independently confirmed real incident: settings.json.recovered exists in userData (dated 2026-07-18), proving Tony's settings.json genuinely became unreadable once and silently fell back to defaults with only a log-line, no user-facing notice. Additional findings: several synchronous fs call sites (import-job-store.ts's list(), brain/ingest.ts's periodic reconcile helpers, match-key-cache.ts's per-answer N+1 stat loop, graphify.ts's status re-parse) that violate the lane's otherwise-consistent async discipline and would scale poorly; uncapped Promise.all fan-out in recall.ts's listMeetings/searchMeetings over every file in an OneDrive-synced folder with no concurrency limit (unlike ingest.ts's own EXTRACT_CONCURRENCY=3 precedent); unbounded, never-cleaned corruption-quarantine files by design; and minor data-fragmentation evidence (three separate historical "meetings folder" locations coexisting on Tony's disk).
architecture_notes: Meetings root resolved by resolveMeetingsFolder() (transcripts.ts:580-595): explicit setting, else OneDrive root (detectOneDrive(), macOS: ~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-*) else Documents, + "Métis Meetings". meeting-path.ts (20 lines) is only a basename traversal-guard, not the root resolver. The "brain" (.brain/ under the meetings root, brain/store.ts:25-36) is a plain-JSON-files knowledge store deliberately co-located with transcripts to inherit OneDrive sync and the same at-rest envelope encryption (ATKENC2 = AES-256-GCM content key wrapped via OS keychain, ATKENC1 legacy safeStorage-direct) — this same encryption scheme also wraps settings.json itself. Two serialization lanes protect concurrent brain mutation: indexLock/updateIndex (ingest.ts:1341-1352) for index.json, withEntityLock (store.ts:279-289) for person/account/deal/graph entity files — both correctly implemented with an inline comment describing the exact prior production bug each one fixed. History/Recall is served by recall.ts's listMeetings/searchMeetings, which async-read+cache every meeting file by (mtime,size) — well designed at the per-file level but with no cap on total files touched per call. Real on-disk evidence gathered: live meetings folder 360 files/892K (59 .md, 283 .brain/*.json, 18 orphan .tmp); legacy "AskToto Meetings" sibling (361 files, OneDrive online-only placeholders, 0B local) preserved by design (copy-forward is additive-only, never deletes source); a third orphaned ~/Documents/Métis Meetings containing only bookkeeping files, evidence of an earlier OneDrive-detection state producing a different root.

findings.failure_scenario: Given the app's own crash/force-quit pattern (lead's E2/E3/E6/E9), several import jobs can plausibly sit in non-terminal state at once; recover() blocks the main-process event loop synchronously proportional to N checkpoints x their size, contradicting the async-everywhere discipline used elsewhere in this same lane (e.g. recall.ts's async readMeeting).

verification.evidence:
The cited code is real, but it does not explain either of Tony's bugs, and P1 is too high.

What the finding gets right:
- src/main/import-job-store.ts:24-49: EncryptedImportJobStore.list() runs readdirSync, statSync and readSavedFile inside one loop with no await in it. So the whole scan finishes in a single main-thread tick.
- src/main/transcripts.ts:325-326: readSavedFile is readFileSync plus decodeSaved. When the envelope is encrypted, decodeSaved goes through tryDecodeSaved and decryptEnvelopeV2 (transcripts.ts:286-309). encryptTranscripts defaults to true (see default-provider.contract.test.ts:76).
- import-jobs.ts:300-336: recover() calls it once, through `await this.deps.store.list()`.

What does not hold:
1. It runs once per boot, and not while the app is painting. index.ts:9314-9323 fires recover() fire-and-forget, after createWindow, after clearBootWatchOnce('createWindow') at 9291 and after IPC registration, and only once requireAuth() passes. It retries every 1 s until then. On any later call, `this.loaded` short-circuits to the in-memory list (import-jobs.ts:301).
2. It is not on the History path. The renderer's IPC.importJobsList handler (index.ts:8323-8327) returns importJobs.list(), which is the in-memory Map (import-jobs.ts:338-340) and touches no disk. The only disk read is at boot. So it cannot cause "clicking History freezes the app".
3. On Tony's machine the store is empty. ~/Library/Application Support/asktoto/import-jobs exists but holds 0 files and 0 B. On the machine that shows the bug, the loop reads nothing.
4. "Unbounded" overstates it. Checkpoints are deleted once a job ends done or cancelled (import-jobs.ts:318, 389, 416, 890; cancel at 415-416). Only in-flight jobs and failed jobs the user has not dismissed stay on disk: fail() at ~996-1004 saves the job but does not delete its checkpoint, and remove() at 437-443 deletes it on dismiss. Each file holds transcript text only, no PCM: roughly 100-500 KB for a multi-hour recording. Reading, AES-GCM decrypting and JSON-parsing a few of those takes single-digit milliseconds. That is a small one-time hitch after first paint, not a freeze. The app's own crash and force-quit pattern does not add files either: recover() puts interrupted jobs back in the queue and runs them to a terminal state rather than piling them up.
5. The suggested fix would not fully deliver. Moving to fs/promises would make only the file reads async. The decrypt step (decryptEnvelopeV2 and its safeStorage key unwrap) and JSON.parse would still run synchronously on the main thread.

Verdict: the code quality point is valid, since this is sync I/O in a main-process async function. The P1 severity and the related_bug=history-freeze link are refuted.
verification.corrected_mechanism_or_fix: Mechanism: this is a one-time synchronous scan at boot. It runs after the window is created, reads only in-flight and not-yet-dismissed failed checkpoints, and costs a few milliseconds at realistic sizes. It is not linked to the History freeze or to the "heavy on the PC" report; look for the History-freeze cause somewhere else. Optional low-priority cleanup: switch list() to `await readdir(root, { withFileTypes: true })` and `await readFile(path)`, then call decodeSaved(buf). Also consider having recover() expire, or cap how many, failed checkpoints the user never dismisses (for example, older than 30 days) so the count cannot grow for ever. Do not make this a P1 fix.

summary: Audited main-process capture/speech lane (screen-capture*, screen-preprocess, apple-speech, asr-*, cloud-stt/, listening-state-ipc, foreground-watcher, platform-perms, island/, calendar, act1-dom-probe, import-audio, whisper-import) against HEAD 2bf21f1c (v1.9.6). Verified both runtime-evidence questions the lead asked about: E5 (background capture.failed-every-6s loop) is CONFIRMED FIXED at HEAD for macOS (screen-preprocess.ts's captureAllowed()/screenCaptureGranted gate, MQA-178/MQA-209, landed 2026-08-19) — but that fix is macOS-only; Windows has no equivalent gate wired (screenCaptureGranted is `undefined` off-darwin in index.ts), so the same forever-6s-loop pattern can still reproduce on Windows if the OS-level per-app screen-capture toggle is denied — a new P1 finding not caught by the sibling B2-resource-heavy audit. E6 (unhandledRejection "Failed to get sources.") is CONFIRMED FIXED at HEAD via 3-layer defense (getScreenSourcesWithRetry's internal catch-all in this lane's screen-capture.ts, a safe-callback wrapper, and an outer "absolute backstop" try/catch), landed 2026-07-06 — flagged as an open question that the evidence's Aug10-Sep16 crash dates postdate that fix, likely due to audit-log cross-version accumulation rather than a live gap. Also found a genuine correctness/data-loss bug in cloud-stt/adapter.ts (Nova-3 normalizer throws and silently discards real final transcript text instead of the "keep text" behavior its own comment documents, untested), a reliability gap in cloud-stt/live-session.ts (no reconnect when a single WS track drops mid-meeting), an architecture fragility in whisper-import.ts (module-global language-follow state safe only because of an unenforced external concurrency=1 clamp in out-of-lane import-jobs.ts), and two minor performance notes (apple-speech.ts spawns a helper process per audio window; island/cursor-watch.ts polls the cursor continuously at ~41Hz). Cross-referenced rather than duplicated B2's already-thorough coverage of foreground-watcher.ts's crash-orphan risk (same root cause as its llama-server/fm-server F1 finding).
architecture_notes: Lane code quality is high overall: heavy dependency injection making core engines (screen-preprocess, foreground-watcher, act1-dom-probe) Electron-free and unit-testable; hash-pinned, resumable, disk-headroom-checked model downloads (asr-model-download.ts, asr-bundled-ensure.ts); real security hardening on the asr-model:// custom protocol (symlink-escape guard, path-traversal rejection); a consistent MQA-numbered fix ledger in comments that made git-archaeology verification of the lead's runtime evidence tractable. The recurring structural pattern worth flagging to the planner: several places in this lane have a well-designed bounded-retry/gating policy sitting right next to a structurally identical mechanism that lacks the equivalent policy — foreground-watcher.ts's MAX_RESTARTS/backoff vs. cloud-stt/live-session.ts's no-restart-on-track-drop; macOS's live screenCaptureGranted permission gate vs. Windows' absent one in screen-preprocess.ts. Fixing these is less "invent new policy" and more "propagate the policy that already exists elsewhere in the same file tree."

findings.title: E5's forever-6s capture.failed loop is only fixed for macOS; Windows has no equivalent screen-capture-permission gate
findings.evidence: captureAllowed() = () => !deps.screenCaptureGranted || deps.screenCaptureGranted() (screen-preprocess.ts:196); index.ts:3893-3896 wires screenCaptureGranted only for darwin, leaving it `undefined` on every other platform, so captureAllowed() unconditionally returns true on Windows. platform-perms.ts:1-7 documents that Windows also has a persistent, revocable per-app screen-recording privacy toggle, and already exposes windowsScreenStatus()/screenProbeResult (platform-perms.ts:78-91) that was simply never wired in.
findings.failure_scenario: A Windows user denies Métis's screen-recording privacy toggle. backgroundScreenContext stays on and the local model/OCR + foreground watcher stay healthy, so eligible() stays true forever. onRefreshTick fires every REFRESH_INTERVAL_MS=6000, describeForWindow calls getScreenshot('bg-screen'), desktopCapturer.getSources() keeps failing, and index.ts's unconditional auditLog('capture.failed', {phase:'bg-screen'}) writes a record every 6 seconds indefinitely — reproducing E5's x5394-line pattern on Windows even though it is fixed on macOS.
findings.fix_direction: Wire a Windows branch of screenCaptureGranted into the createScreenPreprocess(...) call in index.ts using platform-perms.ts's existing windowsScreenStatus(), analogous to the darwin branch; treat the probe's 'unknown' state as not-granted (gate closed) per platform-perms.ts's own 'never assume granted' comment.

verification.evidence:
Read at 2bf21f1c.

What holds:
- src/main/screen-preprocess.ts:196. `captureAllowed = () => !deps.screenCaptureGranted || deps.screenCaptureGranted()`. `eligible()` (lines 198-202) is the only gate before a capture.
- src/main/index.ts:3893-3896. `screenCaptureGranted` is set only when `process.platform === 'darwin'` and is `undefined` everywhere else. The comment at 3891 says this is deliberate: "Windows has no queryable screen grant and its capture prompts nothing."
- On win32 the foreground watcher is real (foreground-watcher.ts:156, which spawns PowerShell), so `start()` arms `setInterval(onRefreshTick, REFRESH_INTERVAL_MS=6000)` (lines 147, 379).
- Each tick calls `describeForWindow` (363). The 2500 ms throttle (148, 266) never blocks a 6 s tick. It then calls `getScreenshot('bg-screen')` (272).
- index.ts:3605 hardcodes `accessStatus='granted'` off darwin. `getScreenSourcesWithRetry` (screen-capture.ts:35-51) makes 3 attempts, returns `[]`, and `!src` throws "No screen source available..." (index.ts:3637-3642). `getScreenshot` then calls `auditLog('capture.failed',{phase:'bg-screen'})` without condition (index.ts:3708-3716), and `describeForWindow`'s catch writes `mainLog.warn` (332-334).
- There is no failure latch or backoff anywhere in screen-preprocess.ts (grep for backoff/fail streak finds nothing).
- So if capture fails persistently, it produces one audit record and one warn every 6 s, forever, with up to 3 `getSources` calls per tick. That code path is confirmed.

What is wrong or overstated:
1. The trigger premise is unverified. The Windows privacy toggle is assumed to make Electron's Win32 `desktopCapturer` fail. platform-perms.ts:1-7 and :37 assert that, but index.ts:3891 says the opposite. Chromium's Windows screen capturer (DXGI/GDI) is generally not gated by that toggle. I could not verify this at runtime, so evidence_label DERIVED is right. Other persistent Windows failures reach the same loop anyway (secure desktop or lock screen, disconnected RDP, zero-pixel sources).
2. "Only fixed for macOS" is wrong. The macOS gate only blocks a TCC status other than 'granted'. When TCC reports 'granted' but the running process cannot capture yet (the needs-relaunch state that the code itself documents in screen-capture.ts:79-81 and index.ts:3638-3640), `eligible()` stays true. `captureScreenshotOnce` then throws the darwin "No screen source available... restart Métis" message, and the same 6 s capture.failed loop runs on Tony's platform. The root cause is the missing failure backoff in `describeForWindow` on every platform, not a missing Windows permission check.
3. The proposed fix would cause a regression. The boot reconcile `runStep('refreshScreenPreprocess')` (index.ts:9307) runs before the win32 probe, which is fire-and-forget (`void probeScreenCapture()`, index.ts:9336-9339). If 'unknown' closes the gate, canRun() is false at boot and `start()` never runs. Nothing calls `refresh()` again after the probe settles or after `noteScreenCaptureOutcome(true)` (index.ts:3626), so Windows background context would stay off for the whole session. Also, `windowsScreenStatus` is not exported (platform-perms.ts:86); only `getPlatformPermissions()` is.

Severity goes down to P2. It is log spam plus a small amount of repeated capture work. The Windows trigger is speculative, Tony runs macOS, and E5's actual reason string (the darwin 'denied' message) is already gated at HEAD.
verification.corrected_mechanism_or_fix:
Corrected mechanism: `describeForWindow` has no backoff after a capture failure on any platform. Any capture failure that persists while `eligible()` is true repeats on every 6 s refresh tick, with 3 `getSources` retries, one capture.failed audit record and one warn log each time. This is reachable on macOS in the TCC-'granted'-but-needs-relaunch state, which the darwin-only gate does not cover. On Windows it is reachable for any persistent capture failure; that the privacy toggle causes one is not proven.

Fix (platform-agnostic, in screen-preprocess.ts):
- Track consecutive `getScreenshot` failures, excluding PrivateViewBlockedError.
- After N failures (for example 2), apply exponential backoff (6 s → 12 → 24 … capped at about 5 min), or latch the engine off until the next `refresh()` or `handleWindowChange`.
- Reset on success.

Also either suppress repeat audit records with an identical reason in `getScreenshot` for phase bg-screen, or have preprocess pass a flag and emit one `capture.failed` per streak.

If a win32 gate is also wanted:
- Use `getPlatformPermissions().screenRecording !== 'denied'`, so 'unknown' at boot does not close the gate before the async probe settles.
- Call `refreshScreenPreprocess()` after `probeScreenCapture()` resolves.
- Call it again when `noteScreenCaptureOutcome` flips denied→granted, so the engine can recover.
- Add a test: getScreenshot rejects repeatedly → at most one capture per backoff window and one audit record per failure streak.

findings.title: Nova-3 normalizer discards real final transcript text instead of the 'keep text' behavior its own comment documents
findings.evidence: adapter.ts:404-413: when isFinal is true, alt.transcript is non-empty, but words[] is empty, the code throws CloudSttError('INVALID_STT_TIME') even though the comment directly above says 'Final without word timings — keep text, refuse invented precise attribution.' The only caller (live-session.ts onMessage, :371-442) swallows this as a mainLog.warn and never calls handlers.onFinal for that segment. adapter.test.ts has zero test cases for this input shape (grepped).
findings.failure_scenario: Deepgram/Nova-3 sends a final Results message with a non-empty transcript but an empty/missing words array (a real, documented wire shape for certain finalization events). That spoken content is silently and permanently dropped from the saved meeting transcript for CLOUD_ONLY/enterprise-live Listen users, with only an unread warn-log line as a trace.
findings.fix_direction: For isFinal && !words.length && transcript.trim(), emit one CloudSttFinalSegment carrying the transcript text with cluster:'unknown' and an explicit no-precise-timing marker instead of throwing; add the missing adapter.test.ts case first.

verification.evidence:
I read the code at HEAD 2bf21f1c. The code defect and the mechanism are real. The finding overstates how likely the trigger is, and it misses one extra consequence.

Confirmed by reading the code:
- src/main/cloud-stt/adapter.ts:404-413 is `if (!words.length) { ... if (!isFinal) return interim; if (!transcript.trim()) return empty; // Final without word timings — keep text, refuse invented precise attribution.  throw new CloudSttError('INVALID_STT_TIME') }`. For a final with text but no words, the function throws every time. The comment says the text is kept; the code does the opposite. The comment was added in e3f966d4 on 2026-09-14.
- src/main/cloud-stt/live-session.ts:392-434 (`onMessage`). The throw happens before `onInterim` and `onFinal`, so the text is neither shown live nor saved. The catch at :433-434 only calls `mainLog.warn('[cloud-stt] normalize skipped', ...)`.
- Extra consequence the finding missed (live-session.ts:435-439, 444-470). If this happens while `closeGracefully` is running (`this.closing`), the catch calls `acknowledgeTrackClose(track, false)`. Once all tracks are acknowledged, `completeGracefulClose(timedOut=true)` sets `closed=true` and closes the sockets. `onMessage` returns early after `closed` (:372), so any tail Results still in flight are also dropped, and the stop is reported as incomplete.
- Reachable in the production build. The `cloudSttStart` IPC handler (src/main/index.ts:6575, which calls `startCloudSttLive` at :6609) picks its provider with `effectiveCloudSttProvider`. For CLOUD_ONLY profiles that function falls back to `DEFAULT_CLOUD_ONLY_STT_PROVIDER = 'cloudflare-nova3'` (src/shared/cloud-stt-provider.ts:21-22, :42). Only CLOUD_ONLY / enterprise-live users can reach it.
- No test covers it. adapter.test.ts has only three Nova-3 cases (final with words, interim, control message). Neither adapter.test.ts nor live-session.test.ts has `words: []` or `INVALID_STT` cases.

Not supported:
- The finding says this is a "real, documented wire shape for certain finalization events". I found no evidence for that. In Deepgram's live Results schema, `alternatives[].transcript` is built from `alternatives[].words`, and the URL builder (adapter.ts:207-217) turns on no feature that removes words. I could not check the Cloudflare AI Gateway passthrough live (no network, no node_modules), so how often this happens in production is unverified and is probably rare. This is defensive handling that contradicts its own comment, not a proven path that loses data regularly.
- It has nothing to do with Tony's two runtime reports ("heavy on the PC" and "History freeze/crash") or evidence E1-E9. It only affects cloud Listen, not the local LLM or the sidecars.

Severity: I'm lowering it from P1 to P2. When it happens, the loss is permanent and silent, and it is worse during stop. But the trigger is not shown to happen, and only enterprise CLOUD_ONLY Nova-3 users are exposed.
verification.corrected_mechanism_or_fix:
How it happens: `normalizeNova3ResultsMessage` (adapter.ts:413) throws INVALID_STT_TIME for a final Results message that has text but no words. `CloudSttLiveSession.onMessage` (live-session.ts:433-434) catches it and only logs a warning, so both the interim and the final are dropped. If this happens while the session is closing, the catch also calls `acknowledgeTrackClose(track, false)` (live-session.ts:435-439), which can close the whole session early and drop any tail finals still queued.

Fix:
1. Write the test first in adapter.test.ts: a final (`is_final:true`) Results message with a non-empty `transcript`, `words: []` and top-level `start` and `duration`. Assert it returns one final with the text.
2. In adapter.ts, replace the throw with a single segment:
   - `text` = the transcript, trimmed
   - `cluster` = `clusterId(undefined)`, which returns 'unknown', so no speaker attribution is invented
   - `language` = 'und'
   - timing: `CloudSttFinalSegment` requires `startMs`/`endMs`. Take the coarse message-level times from Deepgram's top-level `start`/`duration` (seconds), converted with `nonNegative()`, turned into ms and shifted by `streamOffsetMs`. Word-level timing is never faked.
   - `id` = `segmentId(scope, messageSequence, 0)`, `revision: 1`
   - If `start`/`duration` are missing, choose one rule and document it: either fall back to a zero-width range at `streamOffsetMs`, or keep the throw but return the text as `interimText` so it is at least shown.
3. Optionally, in live-session.ts, stop treating a normalize error on a non-terminal Results frame during closing as the track being done. Keep waiting for the Metadata terminal evidence instead of calling `acknowledgeTrackClose(track, false)`.
4. Add a live-session.test.ts case for this frame arriving during `closeGracefully`.
